## The battle screen: the player's Pokémon was exactly the height of the screen

Reported in the same message: *"the battle screen is completely bugged, not using
Platinum's battle UI or background at all, and the player's Pokémon is way too
large."* Both halves are true and they are separate problems.

### The scale, which is one missing arm

`resolveBattleScale` picks a per-generation default and had three:

```lua
BATTLE_SCALE_DEFAULT = { front = 1, back = 2 }   -- Gen 1, whose rips are 40x40
BATTLE_SCALE_GEN2    = { front = 1, back = 1 }
BATTLE_SCALE_GEN3    = { front = 1, back = 1 }
```

with no Gen 4 arm, so a Platinum battle fell through to **Gen 1's**, which doubles
the back pic. Measured rather than estimated: `back/390_chimchar.png` is **80×80**,
and 80 doubled is 160 pixels on a battle surface 160 pixels tall. The player's
Pokémon was not "too large" — it was exactly the height of the screen.

The comment above `BATTLE_SCALE_GEN3` predicts this one generation early: *"Gen 3's
are 64x64… doubled they are 128 pixels tall on a 160-pixel screen: the player's
Pokemon filled half the field and ran off the bottom."* Gen 4 is the same bug with
a bigger sprite. Fixed with the same answer, and the resolver checked across all
four:

```
            before                          after
gen 1  front 40px  back  80px        front 40px  back  80px
gen 2  front 48px  back  48px        front 48px  back  48px
gen 3  front 64px  back  64px        front 64px  back  64px
gen 4  front 80px  back 160px  <--   front 80px  back  80px
```

### The UI, which is a feature that does not exist

There is no `Gen4Battle.lua`. `src/battle/` holds `BattleState`, `Damage`,
`Gen3Battle` and the rulesets, and `BattleState` has a Gen 3 layout arm and
nothing for Gen 4 — so a Platinum battle runs on the **Gen 1/2 screen**: Game Boy
name-and-level boxes, the two-panel FIGHT menu, no background. That is not a bug
to fix, it is a screen to write.

**Every asset it needs is already extracted and sitting in the cache**, which is
the useful half of this finding:

```
battle/front, battle/back              493 each, 80x80
battle/shiny_front, battle/shiny_back  the shiny palettes
battle/female_front, battle/female_back, battle/forms
battle/background/                     the battle backdrops
battle/terrain/                        the platforms
battle/healthbox_player_singles.png    128x64
battle/healthbox_player_doubles.png, healthbox_enemy.png, healthbox_safari.png
battle/interface_cursor_*, interface_stock_*, interface_top_stock_*
battle/anim/                           the move animations
battle/ball_throws_*                   every ball, 10 frames each
battle/trainer_backs_*                 Lucas, Dawn, Barry, Cheryl, Riley,
                                       Marley, Mira, Buck -- 5 frames each
battle/type_icons_*                    all 17 types plus the contest categories
battle/substitute_front/back, shadows.png
```

So the Gen 4 battle screen is a rendering job against data that is already on
disk, not another extraction.

### Committed

* `src/ui/Gen4StarterSelect.lua` — Y-up, the cartridge's camera in full, the
  six-step move, the lift on the right axis, no spin.
* `src/battle/BattleState.lua` — `BATTLE_SCALE_GEN4`, and the arm that reaches it.

## Starting the Gen 4 battle screen: where a Sinnoh battle happens

First layer of the screen that will replace the Game Boy one, and deliberately
only that layer: **which background and which two platforms**. Nothing here
draws yet.

### Why the split is where it is

The cartridge's platform sprite templates (`terrain.c`) are
`{x = 336, y = 136}` for the player's side and `{x = -80, y = 88}` for the
foe's — on a 256-pixel screen, both entirely off it. They are the *off-screen
start of the intro slide*, not where the platforms settle, and the settled
positions come out of the intro animation rather than a table. Writing
plausible numbers in their place is exactly the mistake the briefcase camera
was, so the placement half waits until it can be read rather than guessed.

### The rule, whole

```c
background = the map header's own byte, overridden to BACKGROUND_WATER
             for the whole time the player is surfing

terrain    = the TILE BEHAVIOUR under the player, first match wins:
               ICE 32                          -> ice
               TALL_GRASS 2 / VERY_TALL 3      -> grass
               SAND 33                         -> sand
               SNOW 161,162,163,168            -> snow
               MUD 164,165,166,167             -> great_marsh
               CAVE_FLOOR 8                    -> cave
               surfable (16 of them, a FLAG)   -> water
             else sTerrainForBackground[background]
```

Two things worth writing down as numbers rather than ranges: snow is 161–163
*and* 168, with the four mud values sitting between them; and the surfable set
is a flag, not a block — the ordinary bridge over water and the two bike
bridges are surfable at 115, 120 and 124, a long way from the water at 16–21.

**A Gen 4 map stores the behaviour in the cell itself.** `Gen4Maps.mapDef`
writes `word % 256` into the slot Gen 1–3 put a block id in, so `Map:blockAt`
*is* the behaviour here and the Gen 2/3 `Map:cellBehaviour` — which goes through
a tileset's collision table — does not answer at all.

### Time of day applies to six backgrounds, not twenty-three

`BattleSystem_GetBackgroundTimeOffset` switches on the **background** first:
PLAIN, WATER, CITY, FOREST, MOUNTAIN and SNOW take a real offset and everything
else is always 0. An indoor room does not get darker at night — which is also
why the extractor found the indoor palettes listing one "all" entry three times.

This engine's clock has Gen 2's three bands, not Platinum's five, so TWILIGHT
has nothing to come from and `evening` is unreachable until a Gen 4 clock
exists. Said plainly rather than approximated: inventing a twilight window would
put the wrong palette on six backgrounds for however many hours it guessed.

### `battleBackground` now reaches the map def

`MapHeader_GetBattleBG` is the whole of the cartridge's answer, and
`Gen4MapHeaders` has parsed the byte since it was written
(`floor(flags / 128) % 32`) — it was simply never carried onto the def, so
nothing in the engine could say where a Sinnoh battle happens. **Needs the same
re-import as the trainer sight fields.** Measured across all 593 headers:

```
indoors_1 232   indoors_2 73   cave_3 59   cave_2 51   indoors_3 35
plain 28        forest 27      cave_1 21   city 18     mountain 18
distortion_world 12   snow 8   water 6
aaron / bertha / flint / lucian / cynthia   1 each
```

Every value lands in 0..17 — the five Battle Frontier backgrounds never appear
on a map because those battles set their own — and the four Elite Four rooms
plus Cynthia's appear exactly once each, which is the distribution agreeing with
the game rather than merely parsing.

### `tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua`

Three tables that know nothing about each other — the background enum, the
terrain enum and the `gen4_graphics` index — and a name in one but not the
others returns nil and fights on blank paper, which looks exactly like the bug
this is meant to fix. Eight checks, the first two canaries on the enums
themselves because a mistyped one makes every later check pass against the wrong
word:

```
  ok    backgrounds named (BACKGROUND_MAX)          23
  ok    terrains named (TERRAIN_MAX)                24
  ok    backgrounds with no terrain                  0
  ok    terrains named that do not exist             0
  ok    background pictures missing (23 x 3)         0
  ok    platform pictures missing (24 x 2)           0
  ok    map headers naming an unknown background     0
  ok    map headers walked                         593
```

With the cartridge's assets directory as a second argument it also checks every
stated path is really on disk; without it, it says so rather than quietly
skipping.

### Still to come

The placement half — where the two battlers stand, where the four healthboxes
sit, the move menu, the 256×192 layout arm in `BattleState` beside `gen3Layout`.
The art for all of it is already extracted; what is missing is the geometry, and
it is coming out of the intro animation, not out of a guess.

---

## ...and the placement half, which turned out to be readable after all

I said the settled platform positions "come out of the intro animation rather
than a table." They come out of `battle_display.c`, stated outright, and the
rest of the geometry is stated **twice** by tables written for different
systems. So the guessing this was meant to avoid was not necessary.

### The platforms

`sTerrainSpriteTemplates` gives each platform an off-screen start;
`battle_display.c` sets each a settled position:

```c
ManagedSprite_SetPositionXY(terrain, 24 * 8, 8 * 11)   // enemy  (192, 88)
ManagedSprite_SetPositionXY(terrain, 64, 128 + 8)      // player (64, 136)
```

And the two agree in a way that cannot be coincidence: **the y values are
identical to the templates'** — only x slides — and **both sides travel exactly
34 steps of 8 pixels**, `(336 − 64) / 8` and `(192 − −80) / 8`. A third table,
`gEncounterCoords`, lists the same two starts (336 and −80) for a third
purpose. Three statements, one answer.

### The battlers, stated twice

`BATTLER_POS_*` in `include/constants/battle/battle_anim.h` feeds
`sBattleAnimBattlerPositions`; `gBattlerEncounterX` in `ov12_022380BC.c` is a
separate list for the encounter walk-on. Both give the same six x values —
64, 192, 40, 216, 80, 176 — and the check asserts the agreement rather than
trusting either.

```
                    x    y        healthbox
solo player        64  112        192, 116
solo enemy        192   48         58,  36
player slot 1      40  112        192, 103
enemy  slot 1     216   50         64,  16
player slot 2      80  120        198, 132
enemy  slot 2     176   42         58,  45
```

Worth noticing: the foe's two doubles slots are **not level** (50 and 42) — the
far one sits higher up the field — and the player's doubles healthboxes straddle
the solo one at −13 and +16 while the foe's straddle at −20 and +9. All sprite
centres, because the cartridge's cells are centred.

### The check is 17 now

The nine new ones are all two-statements-meeting, plus two that would catch the
one mistake every individual number survives:

```
  ok    platform slide steps, player vs enemy            34 vs 34
  ok    platform slide steps (272px at 8 a frame)        34
  ok    platforms start at the sprite templates' x       336/-80
  ok    platforms settle where battle_display sets them  (64,136) (192,88)
  ok    a platform past the last step stays put          64
  ok    battler x vs gBattlerEncounterX (6 of them)      0
  ok    settled positions off a 256x192 screen           0
  ok    the player's platform is below the foe's         136 vs 88
  ok    each solo battler sits above its own platform    112<136 and 48<88
```

The last two are the ones that catch **the two sides being swapped**, which
every other number in the table survives unchanged.

### What is left

The drawing: a `gen4Layout()` arm in `BattleState` beside `gen3Layout`, a
256×192 surface, and `Gen4Battle.draw` putting the backdrop, the two platforms,
the two battlers and the healthboxes at the positions above. Every number it
needs is now in the file and checked.

---

## The Gen 4 battle screen is on

`BattleState` has a `gen4Layout()` beside `gen3Layout()`, the battle asks for
**256×192**, and `Gen4Battle.draw` puts Platinum's field and its two Pokémon on
it at the cartridge's own positions.

### The four arms, and what they do not touch

```lua
BattleState:gen4Layout()       GameVersion.isGen4()
BattleState:uiSize()           -> 256, 192   for gen4Layout
BattleState:draw()             -> Gen4Battle.draw
BattleState:drawBattleField()  -> Gen4Battle.drawField
```

No wide option here, unlike Hoenn: the DS screen **is** the layout, and there is
no narrower cartridge shape underneath it to widen. Proved across all four
generations with the committed file:

```
gen 1: gen4Layout false  uiSize 160x144
gen 2: gen4Layout false  uiSize 160x144
gen 3: gen4Layout false  uiSize 240x160
gen 4: gen4Layout true   uiSize 256x192
```

### What it draws

**The field.** The backdrop at 0,0 — it is 512 wide because the cartridge
scrolls it and the visible screen is the left half, so drawing it at 0 is the
whole of what a still frame needs. Then the two platforms, through
`platformAt(side, step)`, which slides them in from off-screen and clamps once
they have arrived; a battle that never sets `introSlide` draws them settled. A
cache with no backdrop gets **black**, not the Game Boy's white paper: every
piece of Gen 4 art over it is drawn for a dark field and white would show as a
bright border round each platform.

**The battlers**, at `BATTLER_POS` — the foe first, so where the two overlap the
player's Pokémon is in front, which is what standing nearer the camera means.
Drawn through `BattleState:drawBattlerPic` rather than blitted here, because
that method carries the grow-in scale, the hit shake, the squash and the rotate,
and a second draw path would have none of them.

### What is still the engine's own, and labelled as such

The healthboxes and the message box. **Platinum's healthbox is not a picture
with words on it** — `healthbox.c` composes it from OAM cells at runtime: a name
window of 8×2 blocks, a 6-cell HP gauge, a 12-cell EXP gauge. Drawing it
faithfully means walking its cell bank, which is the next pass.

Until then the screen puts the engine's existing HUD and message box on,
translated by `(48, 48)` — half the difference between 160×144 and 256×192. That
is not a fudge chosen to look right. It lands the Game Boy's enemy panel (tiles
0,0–11,3, i.e. 48,48–136,80) on top of where Platinum's enemy healthbox goes
(centre 58,36, so 6,4–122,68), and its player panel (136,104–208,128) on
Platinum's player box (centre 192,116, so 128,84–256,148). **Both land within a
dozen pixels of the real thing**, which is why a plain centring is worth more
here than a hand-placed guess.

The stand-in half is wrapped in a `pcall` and a `push`/`pop`: a raise inside it
must not take the battle down, because the field and the battlers above it are
already on screen and are the part this file is responsible for — and a
transform left on is the kind of thing that moves the *next* screen instead of
this one.

### Where that leaves it

Platinum's background, Platinum's platforms, Platinum's sprite positions and
Platinum's sprite scale, with the engine's HUD sitting roughly where Platinum's
goes. Next: the healthbox cell bank, and then the move menu.

---

## The three healthboxes had no cell bank, and the order file says which

The battle screen's HUD is still the engine's stand-in, and the reason turned
out to be upstream: `healthbox_enemy`, `healthbox_player_singles` and
`healthbox_player_doubles` all carry `provisionalLayout` in `gen4_graphics` —
**correct pixels, placeholder arrangement.** They are the only three sheets in
the whole 326-entry battle-object archive with no bank at all, which is why the
extracted PNGs are scattered strips rather than a box.

### Why all four existing rules miss them

`Gen4Archives.cellBank` tries named, folder, prefix and sole. **The bank is
named for the box's SHAPE, not for the box**: there is no `healthbox/enemy_cell`
for the named rule to find, and `short_cell` serves three different sheets so no
prefix reaches it either.

pokeplatinum's own `res/graphics/battle/sprites.order` states the pairing
outright, in `anim, cell, sheet` triples:

```
188 healthbox/short_cell.NCER   189 healthbox/enemy.NCGR
191 healthbox/tall_cell.NCER    192 healthbox/player_singles.NCGR
200 healthbox/short_cell.NCER   201 healthbox/player_doubles.NCGR
```

So a fifth rule: **ADJACENT** — the NCER immediately before the sheet.

### Two things that kept it from being a guess

**It needs the sheet's member index, not its name.** A base name is not unique
here: `healthbox/enemy` is members 188, 194 *and* 197. "The member before the
sheet called X" has no single answer; "the member before member N" has exactly
one. So `cellBank` gained an optional third argument and the extractor passes
`group.NCGR`.

**It is not generalised past the caller that asks.** Measured across every
`.order` file in pokeplatinum, only **99 of 1,157 sheets (8.6%)** are preceded
by an NCER at all — it is the layout of this archive and the summary screen's,
not a rule of the format. I nearly wrote it as a general rule off one file,
which is the same shape as the gym-puzzle overgeneralisation from three samples.
Measuring first is what stopped it.

Reported as its own match strength (`adjacent`) so a consumer can tell it apart
from a name match, and tried last because the named and folder rules are
stronger evidence wherever they apply.

### What it changes, measured over every NCGR in the archive

```
unchanged 118    newly resolved 6    changed 0
```

The six are the three healthboxes across their duplicate members, resolving
exactly as the order file pairs them: `enemy` → `short_cell`,
`player_singles` → `tall_cell`, `player_doubles` → `short_cell`.

After a re-import those three come out assembled, and the battle screen can draw
Platinum's own healthboxes instead of the translated Game Boy panels.

---

## The healthboxes, from the cell banks

Decoded `healthbox/short_cell` and `healthbox/tall_cell` straight out of the
cartridge. Each is **one cell of two 64×64 OAM squares side by side** — so an
assembled box is 128×64, and the two banks differ in exactly one thing:

```
short_cell  (enemy, player doubles)   extent 128x64 at (-64, -28)
tall_cell   (player singles)          extent 128x64 at (-64, -32)
```

Those origins are from the sprite centre, which is what `HEALTHBOX_POS` holds,
so a box's top-left is centre + origin. The four-pixel difference between them is
the whole reason there are two banks.

**The second OAM confirms the tile order.** It names tile 32, and Platinum's
mapping mode is 1, so an index steps two tiles: 32 × 2 = 64 — the left square is
tiles 0–63 and the right 64–127. That is what says the blocks are sequential
rather than interleaved, and it is the corroboration the name window needs.

**The name window is the top-left 64×16.** `healthbox.c` writes it at
`HEALTHBOX_NAME_WINDOW_OFFSET 0`, 8×2 blocks of 32 bytes — 16 tiles starting at
tile 0, which with the order above is the first two rows of the left square.

### The two gauges are deliberately not drawn

Their positions are **VRAM byte offsets** — `sHPGaugeVRAMTransfer`, and 1632 /
3584 for the EXP bar — that have to become tiles and then pixels. The arithmetic
is straightforward, but the step from tile number to screen position rests on the
1D row-major layout above, which the OAM corroborates and nothing *second* states
outright.

Every other number on this screen is stated twice. These are not. The thing that
would settle them is looking at the assembled art — which does not exist until
the cell-bank fix has been through an import. So they wait for that rather than
being written down now and checked later.

### How it degrades

`drawHealthboxes` is all-or-nothing on purpose: one Platinum box beside one Game
Boy panel is worse than two of either. A box still flagged `provisionalLayout` is
**declined** rather than drawn — scattered strips where the box goes reads as a
rendering bug, not as a stale cache — and the screen falls back to the engine's
panels exactly as before.

The check reports that state rather than failing on it, because a cache imported
before the cell-bank fix is *expected* to be provisional:

```
  ok    healthboxes that miss the screen entirely     0
  ok    the name window sits inside the box           0,0 64x16 in 128x64
  ok    healthbox art missing or the wrong size       0

NOTE: 2 healthbox(es) are still provisionalLayout in this cache (enemy, player).
      They assemble on the next import; until then the battle screen declines
      them and draws the engine's own panels instead.

20 checks, 0 failures
```

One of those checks is worth naming: a healthbox is **allowed** to run off an
edge — the foe's hangs off the left on the cartridge — so the test is that the
box *overlaps* the screen, not that it is inside it. The tighter test would fail
on correct data.

## Platinum's message box, and a frame reader that disagreed with itself

The battle screen's text area was the last piece still wearing the Game Boy's
clothes: a 160x144 box translated into the middle of a 256x192 screen. It is
Platinum's own now, and every number came out of the cartridge.

### The window is stated four times

```
battle_main.c:465    Window_Add(bgConfig, windows,     1, 2, 19, 27, 4, 11, 31)
battle_main.c:559    Window_Add(bgConfig, &windows[0], 1, 2, 19, 27, 4, 11, 31)
battle_main.c:1682   Window_Add(bgConfig, window,      1, 2, 19, 27, 4, 11, 31)
field_message.c      FieldMessage_AddWindow(..., 2, 19, 27, 4, ...)
```

Left 2, top 19, 27 tiles wide, 4 tall — the **text interior**, so x 16..232 and
y 152..184. The battle box and the overworld box are the same box.

`DrawMessageBoxFrame` then wraps it, and its caps are **unequal**: two tiles on
the left, three on the right, one row above and one below. On a 32-tile screen
that means the frame is **columns 0..31, rows 18..23** — the full width of the
DS screen, 48 pixels deep.

Two lines of sixteen, and the sixteen is stated too: `FONT_MESSAGE` is
`maxLetterHeight = 16, lineSpacing = 0`, and a four-tile window is 32 tall.
`BattleSystem_ShowMessage` prints at offset (0, 0) inside it — four separate
call sites all passing zeroes — so the first line starts at the window's own
origin.

### The bug this uncovered was in the *field* box

`gen4DialogueBox` in `src/render/Font.lua` carried this comment:

> the box reaches one tile past the left of the rectangle it is given and two
> past the right, exactly as the cartridge draws it around a window

and the loop underneath drew strictly inside `[tx, tx + tw)`. **The comment was
right and the code was wrong.** The whole eighteen-tile pattern was being
squeezed into the port's rectangle, so both caps landed three columns in from
where Platinum puts them — on the overworld box as much as anywhere, since it
is the same reader.

Fixed to `tw + 3` columns starting at `tx - 1`. Sinnoh's field box is the case
that proves it: the theme turns `(2, 19) 27x4` into `tx = 1, tw = 29`, and
`tx - 1 = 0` with `tx + tw + 1 = 31` is exactly the 32-tile screen.

`Gen4StarterSelect` and `Gen4RowanIntro` were both drawing a hand-placed
`{ 0, 16, 32, 8 }` — two rows too tall, and once the reader was fixed, one tile
off the screen at each side. Both are on the cartridge's rect now.

### The menus: what is derived and what is staged

`battle_subscreen.c` states the buttons twice over, which is what made them safe
to read. A `TouchScreenRect` is `{ top, bottom, left, right }`:

```
sActionMenuTouchRects              result
  { 0x18, 0x90, 0x00, 0xFF }        1  FIGHT   y  24..144, full width
  { 0x90, 0xC0, 0x00, 0x50 }        2  ITEM    y 144..192, x   0.. 80
  { 0x90, 0xC0, 0xB0, 0xFF }        3  PARTY   y 144..192, x 176..255
  { 0x98, 0xC0, 0x58, 0xA8 }        4  RUN     y 152..192, x  88..168

sBattleMenuButtonLayout[2][3] = { {0,0,0}, {1,3,2} }
```

The keypad grid and the x ranges agree: FIGHT spans the top, and underneath,
left to right, ITEM, RUN, PARTY. The move list is the same shape —
`sMoveMenuButtonLayout[3][2] = { {1,2}, {3,4}, {0,0} }` over four rects that
split at 128 of 256, exactly half, with a full-width cancel bar below.

Those rectangles are a whole second screen. Drawn over the main screen they
would cover the battle; drawn on the second screen they are the cartridge's
picture exactly, which is where they belong and what `src/ui/SecondScreen.lua`
is for. **That route is the next piece of work and these constants are what it
will use.**

Until then the menus go where every other version in the launcher puts them —
inside the message box, two columns instead of three. Folding the cartridge's
bottom row leaves ITEM then PARTY with RUN last:

```
FIGHT      BAG
POKeMON    RUN
```

which is the order `Gen3Battle` reads out of Emerald's own menu string. The
agreement is the point: BAG and POKeMON do not swap places when a player
crosses from Hoenn to Sinnoh in this launcher.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **35 checks, 0 failures** — fifteen of
them new, and they assert the arithmetic rather than the literals, so a nudged
row has to disagree with `DrawMessageBoxFrame` to get past them.

## The second import landed the healthboxes

```
healthbox_player_singles   128x64  cellBank "healthbox/tall_cell"   cellMatch "adjacent"
healthbox_enemy            128x64  cellBank "healthbox/short_cell"  cellMatch "adjacent"
healthbox_player_doubles   128x64  cellBank "healthbox/short_cell"  cellMatch "adjacent"
healthbox_safari           128x64  cellBank "healthbox/safari_cell" cellMatch "named"
```

No `provisionalLayout` anywhere. The fifth "adjacent NCER" rule fired exactly as
designed, and the named rule still caught the safari box on its own.

### Which unblocks the two gauges — and they now have three statements each

These were deliberately left undrawn because the step from tile number to screen
position rested on the 1D row-major layout, which the OAM corroborated but
nothing stated twice. The assembled art settles it, and two more sources agree:

**Measured off the art.** In all three boxes the brown trough is rows 31..38,
and inside it, on rows 35 and 36, there is a dark channel of exactly:

```
healthbox_player_singles   x  72..119   48 px      EXP: row 50, x 24..119, 96 px
healthbox_enemy            x  56..103   48 px      (no EXP bar)
healthbox_player_doubles   x  64..111   48 px      (no EXP bar)
```

**Stated in the cartridge.** `HEALTHBOX_HP_CELL_COUNT 6` and
`HEALTHBOX_EXP_CELL_COUNT 12`, with `CalcGaugeFill`'s own comment saying
*"gauges have 8 pixels per 'square' of fill"* — 6 x 8 = 48, 12 x 8 = 96.

**Stated again in the VRAM table.** `sHPGaugeVRAMTransfer`'s two runs per box
sum to `0xC0` bytes = 6 tiles, in the same `{ position, size }` format the name
window's transfers use.

Three independent sources, one answer. The fill maths comes with them:

```
pixels = cur * width / max          (integer division, and FillCells /
                                     App_PixelCount both force a minimum of
                                     1 pixel while cur > 0)
colour = App_BarColor(pixels, width):
           pixels > width/2  -> GREEN
           pixels > width/5  -> YELLOW
           pixels > 0        -> RED
```

Note the colour is chosen from **pixels, not HP** — so the ramp steps where the
bar steps, not where the fraction does.

And the cartridge states which box shows what, outright:

- enemy boxes: never current HP, max HP or the EXP bar
- player doubles: never the EXP bar, and it toggles between the HP bar and the
  raw numbers on `numberMode`
- player solo: never the caught-species pokeball

**The one thing still missing is the three fill colours.** The green, yellow and
red ramps live in the healthbox parts blob that `GetHealthBoxPartsTile` reads,
and nothing in the graphics stage extracts it yet — `gen4_graphics` has the four
box frames and the ten arrow frames and no parts sheet. That is one extractor
stage, and it is what the gauges are waiting on now. The geometry and the maths
above are settled and are not waiting on anything.

## The gauges, and the array that was never in an archive

The three fill ramps turned out not to be missing from the extraction — they
were never extractable by the machinery doing the extracting. `healthbox.c`
reaches them through

```
GetHealthBoxPartsTile(part) -> &sHealthBoxPartsBitmap[part * 32]
```

and `sHealthBoxPartsBitmap` is
`#include "res/graphics/battle/healthbox/healthbox_parts.4bpp.h"` — **a plain
array compiled into the battle overlay**. A stage that walks NARCs was never
going to find it. 78 tiles in `enum HealthBoxPart` order: the four gauge ramps,
the "HP" glyphs, the slash, two digit strips, the bar end, six status icons, the
gendered "Lv" cells and the caught-species ball.

### Found by structure, not by address

A hard offset is a fact about one build, so this follows the type chart and the
object-graphics table and *searches*. The signature is derived from the enum, so
no cartridge bytes are written into the port:

1. `GREEN_FILL_0`, `YELLOW_FILL_0` and `RED_FILL_0` are the **same tile** — an
   empty gauge looks the same whatever colour it would have filled in — and the
   enum spaces the ramps exactly nine tiles apart. Three identical 32-byte
   blocks, 288 bytes apart. That's the prefilter.
2. Within a ramp, tile *k* differs from tile 0 in exactly *k × rows* nibbles:
   one more pixel column per step. Four ramps must verify at +2, +11, +20 and
   +29 tiles.

Property 1 alone matches **542 times** across the cartridge. Property 2 alone
matches **four times**, and all four are the four ramps, consecutive, in
**overlay 16** — the battle overlay. Together: exactly one hit in the ARM9 and
all 122 overlays.

**The structural test also caught an off-by-one-word that a hand-read wouldn't
have.** My first reading by eye put the blob four bytes earlier. Both alignments
pass a naive ramp test, because the differing rows sit in the middle of the
tile. The tiebreaker is that on the correct alignment the EXP ramp varies in
exactly **one** row and the HP ramps in exactly **two** — which is what a
one-pixel and a two-pixel bar must do. The wrong alignment made the EXP ramp
appear to vary in two.

### And then the alignment proved itself

The gauge is a tile substitution in the healthbox sprite's character data, so it
*must* land on the box's own 8×8 grid. The parts tile puts the HP bar on its
rows 3–4 and the EXP bar on its row 2, so the tiles' tops sit at box rows
`35 − 3 = 32` and `50 − 2 = 48`.

```
HP  gauge   singles x=72  enemy x=56  doubles x=64   y=32
EXP gauge   singles x=24                             y=48
```

**All six are multiples of eight.** Six numbers measured off a picture with no
knowledge of that constraint, and all six satisfy it.

### The fill indices, straight out of the ramps

| ramp | empty | filled | bar rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| HP green | 5 | 6 | 3–4 |
| HP yellow | 5 | 8 | 3–4 |
| HP red | 5 | 10 | 3–4 |
| EXP | 14 | 12 | 2 |

Nothing needs those numbers at runtime — the screen blits the tile — but they
are what makes the reading checkable, and they are why the parts sheet is
composed with the **healthbox family's own palette**: the greens, yellows and
reds come out of the cartridge rather than being chosen to look close.

### What the screen does with them

`Gen4Battle.drawGauges` draws each gauge as its `cells` tiles side by side,
picking one of `FILL_0..FILL_8` per cell — which is exactly what `DrawGauge`
does. The maths is the cartridge's:

```
pixels = floor(cur * width / max)      -- and FillCells / App_PixelCount BOTH
                                       -- force a minimum of 1 while cur > 0
ramp   = App_BarColor(pixels, width):  -- note: PIXELS, not HP
           > width/2 green, > width/5 yellow, > 0 red
```

Because the colour is chosen from pixels rather than the fraction, the ramp
steps where the *bar* steps — a Pokémon on 25.1% shows yellow only once the bar
has actually fallen to ten pixels.

The EXP bar asks `BattleState:expFraction` rather than working the level out
again, which is what keeps it agreeing with the Gen 3 screen's bar while a
level-up animation runs.

And which box shows what is the cartridge's rule, not a choice — `HealthBox_Draw`
clears `HEALTHBOX_INFO_NOT_ON_ENEMY` for all three enemy types and
`HEALTHBOX_INFO_EXP_GAUGE` for both doubles slots. So the HP numbers moved from
"the player's box" to the player's **solo** box, where the cartridge puts them.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **39 checks, 0 failures**, and the gauge
block re-measures rather than restates: every gauge coordinate is checked
against the 8×8 grid, every bar against the box it has to fit inside, and the
parts sheet against the enum's own spacing. A cache imported before this stage
existed gets a spoken NOTE and the gauges are declined rather than drawn wrong.

**This needs one more import** — the parts sheet does not exist in the current
cache.

## Three from play: the party menu, the buttons, and the box that was too narrow

### The party menu in a Platinum battle was Kanto's

`Gen4PartyMenu` existed and the field screen used it. The alias in `Screens.lua`
left `battle` out on purpose, on the reasoning that a declined push would be
served by the Gen 3 screen — which already answers SHIFT and forced switches.

**It would not.** `resolveId` asks the Gen 4 table first, and when that declines
it reaches

```lua
local alias = GEN3_ALIASES[id]
if not alias then return id, arg end
if not isGen3(game) then return id, arg end   -- <- a Platinum cache is not Hoenn
```

and hands back the **Game Boy** id. So every in-battle POKéMON press on Platinum
opened Kanto's party list — the same shape as the keyboard and the Pokédex
before it.

Worth writing down as a rule, because it applies to every entry in that table:
**on a Gen 4 cache a declined Gen 4 alias falls to Gen 1, not to Gen 3.** There
is no middle rung. `tmhm`, `chooseOrder` and `onOrder` are still declined and
still land on the Game Boy screen; the only fix for those is to write the Gen 4
flow.

What made serving `battle` honest rather than a dead end: out of a battle the
submenu's second row is SWITCH and it reorders the party, which in a fight is a
dead end. In a battle the first row is now **SEND OUT** and hands the member
straight back. Whether it *may* go out stays `BattleState`'s question — its own
`onSwitch` already rejects an egg, a fainted member and one already on the
field, says so and reopens the screen — so those three tests are not duplicated
here where they could drift.

### The box was too narrow because the frame reader was

Reported as *"its too skiny text is overlapping the borders"*, and both halves
are the same bug: `gen4DialogueBox` drew the eighteen-tile pattern inside the
rect it was given instead of reaching past it. Before:

```
frame   x 8..240      (29 columns, caps 3 in from where they belong)
text    x 16..232     -> straight over the right cap at 216
```

After, with the reader drawing `tw + 3` columns from `tx - 1`:

```
frame   x 0..256      left cap at 0, right cap at 232..255
text    x 16..231     clear of both
```

One latent fault came out with it. `Data.lua` publishes `maxPixels` beside
`maxCols` for the DS box and explains in its own comment that *"maxPixels is the
part that actually stops the spill"* — and `TextBox` only ever read
`opts.maxPixels`, never the theme's. On Platinum the two happen to agree at 216
so nothing was visibly wrong, but any theme whose fields disagree wrapped to the
wrong one. It reads both now.

### The buttons: the whole bottom screen is seven tilemaps

*"make it match the color and style that would be in the bottom screen"* — and
the reason they never did is that Platinum's FIGHT, BAG, POKéMON and RUN buttons
are not sprites. They are **tilemaps**, and the sprite-shaped machinery in the
graphics stage had no reason to look for them.

They are in `pl_batt_bg.narc` — the **same archive as the battle backdrops**,
which is why they were hiding in plain sight:

```
tiles      member 28    (169 in the Frontier)
palette    member 242   (340 in the Frontier)
tilemaps   49, 42, 47, 43, 44, 48, 45   (sBgScreenNarcIndices' order)
```

Composed and looked at, they are:

| member | what it is |
|---|---|
| 49 | the pale panel with the Poké Ball watermark |
| 42 | the big **red FIGHT** button, with orange BAG, blue RUN and green POKéMON beneath |
| 47 | four grey move slots — the empty state |
| 43 | four move buttons with type-coloured frames, over the blue cancel bar |
| 44 | the pressed states of the same four |
| 48 | the purple selection outlines |
| 45 | the target-select / message panel |

The cartridge names none of them — it copies all seven into buffers and swaps
them onto the four sub BG layers as the menu changes — so those labels are the
port's, given after composing each one. That split is stated in the module
rather than implied. **The button positions agree with `sActionMenuTouchRects`
to the pixel**, which is two unrelated readings of the same screen landing in
the same place.

#### The per-background palette replaces sub-palette ZERO, not one

`BattleSubscreen_New` loads member 242 whole, then loads
`sSubscreenBgPlttIndices[bg].bgPlttIndex` with `srcSize = PALETTE_SIZE_BYTES`
and `destStart = PLTT_DEST(0)` — thirty-two bytes into destination zero. One
sub-palette, over the first.

Reading that as sub-palette 1 is not a harmless slip. I tried it first and the
FIGHT button came out cream-on-black instead of red, because the action layer's
cells are on sub-palettes 1 to 4 and every one of them was being overwritten.
Measured, which is what settled it — the sub-palettes each tilemap's cells
actually name:

```
base 0 | action 1,2,3,4 | moves_idle 13 | moves 0,3,4,8,9,10,11
moves_pressed 0,2,3,4,5,6,12,13 | cursor 0 | panel 0,1,4
```

So **the action menu is the same red, orange, blue and green in every battle**,
and what recolours with the backdrop is the panel behind it. Which is the right
way round: you learn where BAG is once.

The stage writes each fixed layer once and each recolouring layer once per
background — 92 pictures. `tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **46 checks, 0
failures**, and the one that earns its place asserts that every touch rectangle
lies on the screen the art draws.

**Still to do:** the menus are extracted but not yet drawn from. That is the
`SecondScreen` route — the same constants, on the bottom-screen surface Cedric's
original brief asks for — and it is the next piece of work.

## Two presentations of one menu

From the brief: *"when the bottom screen is up show the fight run bag and
pokemon buttons on there but when they have it put away draw the button tiles
next to the text box on the bottom of the screen in the same art style but fit
to the text boxes size"*.

So there are two presentations, and the point is that they **share their art**.

### Which one, decided before anything is drawn

That order matters more than it sounds. The compact buttons *are* the bottom
strip — laying them inside a message-box frame reads as a mistake, and the
buttons carry their own borders already — so the frame has to be skipped, which
means the presentation has to be known before the first thing is drawn.

```
"bottom"    the cartridge's whole picture on the second screen; the strip
            here keeps the message box
"compact"   put away: the same four buttons nine-sliced into the strip, no
            frame under them
"words"     no subscreen art in this cache: the labels in the box, which is
            what this screen did before the art existed
```

**A DS's bottom screen is on until you put it away**, so in a battle it counts
as up until the player has touched the hotkey — `game.secondScreenUp` is nil
until then, and nil is not the same answer as false. Outside a battle the
field's rule (raised only when toggled) is unchanged; this is a battle's reading
of the same flag, and it lives in `Gen4Battle` rather than `SecondScreen`
because that module deliberately owns no per-screen policy.

### Fitting a 216×93 button into a 28-pixel slot

Scaling would squash the bevel and the highlight along with everything else. A
**nine-slice** keeps the corners and the top and bottom bands at their own size
and stretches only the flat middle — which is how this engine already redraws
the dialogue frame at any width.

The corner inset was measured by walking the first rows of each button and
watching the opaque run move in:

```
BAG     9, 8, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0 ...
FIGHT   13, 12, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0 ...
MOVE    8, 7, 3, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0 ...
```

The curve is done by the sixth row and the widest overhang is the first, so the
inset is that first number — the smallest nine-slice that contains the whole
corner *and* the bevel above it. It is clamped against the target as well as the
source, because the strip asks for buttons shorter than twice the corner.

### What is derived and what is chosen

**Derived** — the compact strip's *columns* are the cartridge's own, straight
out of `sActionMenuTouchRects`: FIGHT spans the width, and under it BAG at
x 0..80, RUN at 88..168, POKéMON at 176..255. Those columns are why the strip
reads as Platinum's at a fifth of the height.

**Chosen** — the *vertical* split. The cartridge gives FIGHT 71% of a 168-pixel
column; compressed into a strip, that same share leaves the three small buttons
15 to 18 pixels tall, and the dialogue face is **sixteen**. So the strip is
halved instead. That is the one number here that was picked rather than read,
and it is picked for the only reason that matters at this size: the words have
to fit inside the buttons. The strip is 64 pixels rather than the message box's
48 for the same reason — 48 halved is 24, and a 24-pixel button with a 9-pixel
corner at each end has six pixels of middle.

The checks test both halves in the way each deserves: the derived columns
against `ACTION_RECTS`, and the chosen rows against the constraint they were
chosen for — *every compact button holds a 16-pixel line*. Checking a number
that was picked against its own reason is the only honest test of it.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **54 checks, 0 failures**.

### The selected button

The cartridge marks a pressed button by swapping in a whole second tilemap
(`moves_pressed`), and there is no pressed art for the action buttons at all —
so the highlight is the port's own and is said to be. A wash rather than a
border, because the buttons already have borders and a second one reads as a
glitch.

---

## The hotkey the two presentations were waiting on

The two presentations shipped without a way to choose between them, which I
should have noticed while writing them: the only thing in the whole port that
touched `game.secondScreenUp` was the field's L key opening the Poketch, which
sets it true on open and **false on close**.

So the flag a battle was reading meant "the Poketch is on screen right now", not
"the player wants the bottom screen". A player who had looked at the Poketch
once in the field left it false behind them, and every battle afterwards came up
with its menu stowed — with no way back, because nothing in a battle ever set it
again.

**`raised` and `stowed` are different questions.**

- `raised` is transient and belongs to whatever is on the bottom surface right
  now. That is the right shape for a screen you *open*.
- `stowed` is the player's standing answer to "do I want the bottom screen at
  all". A battle's menu is not something you open — it is where the menu lives
  until you say otherwise.

`stowed` lives in the save rather than on the session, because a choice about
how the game looks should survive closing it. `mode == "off"` is still the
stronger statement — no second surface ever, which is also what keeps every
Gen 1–3 battle on the path it has always had; `stowed` is "not just now".

### One key, one meaning

**L shows or hides the bottom screen.** In the field that surface is the
Poketch; in a battle it is the FIGHT/BAG/POKéMON/RUN menu and the move list. L
rather than a new binding for the same reason the Poketch uses it — it is an
action the controls menu already lists, so it is rebindable without either
screen knowing how rebinding works.

The handler sits at the top of `BattleState:update` rather than inside the menu
branch, because **both** choosing phases put something on that surface and a key
that worked on one and not the other would read as a bug. It does nothing in any
other phase: while a message is typing there is nothing down there to hide.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **62 checks, 0 failures**, and the new
eight drive the seam directly — that `off` means stowed and cannot be
un-stowed (the Gen 1–3 guarantee), that a second screen starts **up**, that L
toggles it both ways, that the choice lands in the save and not on the session,
and that it never touches the Poketch's transient flag.

---

## Everything at the bottom of the screen was missing for one reason

Reported from play: the text box, the FIGHT / BAG / POKéMON / RUN buttons and
the move list were **all** absent in single-screen mode. Three symptoms, one
cause, and it is a trap this project has already paid for once.

```lua
function Gen4Battle.drawTextArea(battle)    -- line 750
  ...
  up, SecondScreen = bottomScreenUp(battle.game)   -- line 774
...
local function bottomScreenUp(game)          -- line 1070
```

**A file-local referenced above its `local function` line is not that local.**
Lua resolves the name as a global, finds nil, and the call raises — every menu
frame, every move-select frame.

And it was invisible because the guard worked. `Gen4Battle.draw` wraps the text
area in a `pcall` so a fault there cannot take the field and the battlers down
with it; the fault was caught, the bottom of the screen stayed blank, and it
read as *"the text box was never written"* rather than *"the text box is
crashing"*. The guard is right; the silence was not. It now says so once —
once, because it raises sixty times a second and a log that scrolls is a log
nobody reads.

This is the same shape as `itemKey` in `Gen4Commands`, where every
`buffertmhmmovename` in the game raised. Both were found by reading, eventually.
So there is now `tools/lua_use_before_local.py`, which finds them by looking:
for each `local function NAME`, is there a `NAME(` at a lower line number? It
strips strings and comments first — a first cut matched `"...missing (23 x 3)"`
and a checker with false positives is one people learn to skip — and it carries
a canary, because a scanner that matches nothing passes everything.

**198 files scanned, 0 sites, canary ok.**

## The healthbox lettering

### The name was being drawn off the left of the screen

`HEALTHBOX_NAME` was 8×2 blocks from tile 0 — which is where the cartridge's
name window lives in the sprite's **character data**. The assembled picture is
the **cell bank's** arrangement of that data, and the two are not the same grid.
Drawing at the picture's (0,0) put the name on the box's decorative tail, and on
the foe's box that tail hangs off the left edge of the screen. The name was at
x = −4.

So the panel is measured off the art instead — the green field above the brown
trough, which comes out as a clean rectangle in each box:

```
healthbox_player_singles   x 23, y 16, 105 x 15
healthbox_enemy            x  6, y 17, 106 x 14
healthbox_player_doubles   x 15, y 17, 107 x 14
```

All three ~106 × 14, which is the consistency that says they are right. They
differ in where they start because the tails differ — the player's on the left,
the foe's on the right — which is exactly why one rect could never have served
all three.

### It is not set in the dialogue face

The cartridge says so three times: `HealthBox_DrawBattlerName`,
`DrawLevelNumber` and `DrawMaxHP` all print with **`FONT_SYSTEM`**, not
`FONT_MESSAGE` (healthbox.c 1143, 1316, 1355). The cache already publishes both
— `faces.system` beside `pages.message` — and `Font.pushFace` is how a screen
picks one. It was using the message face, which is the one every other screen in
the port uses.

The level is placed first and the name fitted to what is left, so a long
nickname is cut rather than printed through the level.

### The HP numbers are not text at all

`HealthBox_DrawCurrentHP` blits `HEALTHBOX_PART_NUMBERS_LEFT`, `_NUMBERS_RIGHT`
and `_SLASH` out of the parts blob (healthbox.c 840–845) — digit **tiles**. The
measurement that proves it: the band they sit in, between the trough's last row
and the EXP groove, is **nine rows deep**, and the system face is sixteen. They
are right-aligned in that band and centred vertically for now; the real digits
arrive with the parts sheet, the same import the gauges are waiting on.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **68 checks, 0 failures**.

## Still open, and precisely

- **The green HP bar** — the ramps are in the parts sheet. One import.
- **The party icons** — `/poketool/icongra/pl_poke_icon.narc` is **not extracted
  at all**. `data.icons` is nil on a Platinum cache, so `Gen4PartyMenu:iconFor`
  returns nothing and every slot falls back to the ball. That is a new extractor
  stage, and the same one serves the summary page, the box and the Poketch's
  party-status app.
- **The summary page's front sprite** — different cause. `gen4_species_sprites`
  *is* extracted; `Gen4SummaryMenu` declares a `picture` slot at (20, 70) and
  never draws into it. The screen needs the draw, not the data.

## Backing out of the party screen crashed the battle

```
src/battle/BattleState.lua:9153: attempt to index local 'mon' (a nil value)
  ... BattleState.lua:9153: in function 'onSwitch'
  ... Gen4PartyMenu.lua:127: in function 'handOff'
  ... Gen4PartyMenu.lua:227: in function 'update'
```

**Nil is "I changed my mind", not a Pokémon.** A party screen that is not a
forced switch hands its answer back on B as well as on A — nil for "none" —
because *out of a battle* that is how a caller learns the player cancelled. The
battle's own `onSwitch` was written for the answer and not for the refusal, and
ran straight into `mon.hp`.

Fixed on both sides, which is deliberate:

- The **screen** no longer hands nil to a battle at all. B in a battle is "back
  to the menu", not "I pick nothing", and the battle already knows what to do
  when the screen simply closes — `afterQueue` put it back in the menu phase
  before it opened. Same for the CANCEL row, which is the same refusal by
  another route.
- The **battle** guards `if not mon then return end` anyway. A mod can serve
  `PartyMenu`, and a handler that only works for well-behaved callers is one
  line short of working for all of them.

## "It still shows the large one when I have it turned off"

The logic was right. The *control* was the problem: the only way to put the
bottom screen away was the L hotkey — which works, but is a rebindable key with
no label anywhere in the game, so "turned off" could just as easily have meant
the options menu, and the options menu had nothing to say about it.

**OPTIONS now carries a row that says which:**

```
2ND SCREEN    SWAP / CORNER / OFF     what shape the bottom screen takes
2ND SIZE      35% … 70% / --          only meaningful in CORNER
BATTLE MENU   2ND / STRIP             where the FIGHT menu is right now
```

`BATTLE MENU` toggles the same flag L does, so the two can never disagree, and
it reads `--` when the second screen is off entirely.

### And the decision is a named function now

A decision worth testing is worth naming. The three-way choice lived inline in
`drawTextArea`, which meant the one thing a player can actually get wrong could
only be checked by playing. It is `Gen4Battle.menuPresentation` now, and the
check walks **every** combination of the two settings and the one cache fact —
nine cases, plus the two the report is about asserted on their own so a failure
names itself instead of being one of nine.

Writing that check immediately found a second fault. `hasSubscreenArt` was
asking "did the picture load", which needs a graphics device — so it answered
false in the harness and, more importantly, **conflated two different failures**:

- a cache with no subscreen stage in it has no buttons and will not until the
  next import — that is the `words` presentation, permanently;
- an image that declines to load on one frame is a fault, and the draw returning
  false already puts the frame and the labels down for it.

It asks what the cache *declares* now. A decision nobody can test off-device is
one that gets tested by playing, which is how this whole report started.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **72 checks, 0 failures**.
