## The party icons: an archive nobody had opened

Reported from play: *"in the pokemon party menus the pokemon party sprites are
missing"*. They were not broken — **they were never extracted**. Nothing in the
Gen 4 pipeline had ever opened `/poketool/icongra/pl_poke_icon.narc`, so
`data.icons` was nil on a Platinum cache, `Gen4PartyMenu:iconFor` found nothing,
and every slot fell back to the ball behind it.

### The archive

```
0        NCLR, 256 colours — and only THREE of its sixteen ramps carry any colour
1..6     three NANR/NCER pairs, the bounce animation's cell banks
7..546   one NCGR per icon, 540 of them
```

`IconTilesIndex(icon) = icon + icon_00000_NCGR` (src/pokemon_icon.c), so the
sheet for species N is member 7 + N, and the sheets past the species run are the
forms — Unown's letters, Deoxys, Burmy, Wormadam, Shellos, Gastrodon, Giratina,
Shaymin, Rotom — plus the two eggs. Each sheet is 1072 bytes: a 48-byte header
and 1024 of pixels, which at 4bpp is 32×64 — **two 32×32 frames**, the up and
down of the bounce.

### Which of the three ramps, and an honest tie-break

`PokeIconPaletteIndex` ends `return sPokemonIconPaletteIndex[species]`, and that
array is `#include "res/pokemon/species_icon_palettes.h"` — compiled into the
ARM9, like the healthbox parts. One byte per icon, values 0..2.

Found by structure: a run of at least 540 bytes, every one below the number of
ramps that actually carry colour. Over the whole ARM9 that matches **twice**, so
there is a tie-break, and it is worth stating plainly because it is a judgement
rather than a derivation:

> **The run whose values are most evenly spread wins.**
>
> ```
> the other run   434 / 86 / 20     0.852 bits
> this one        252 / 149 / 139   1.530 bits   (of a possible 1.585)
> ```
>
> A selector that puts eighty per cent of the species on one ramp is not
> selecting.

That reasoning is suggestive and not proof, so **the answer was checked by
looking**: a hundred icons rendered with it come out the right colours —
Bulbasaur green, Charmander orange, Squirtle blue, Pikachu yellow, Mewtwo
purple, the three Sinnoh starters, Dialga, Palkia, Giratina, Arceus. With the
other run every one of those seven lands on ramp 0, which cannot be right for
two species of different colours.

`tools/gen4_icon_check.lua` then asserts the seven values that render was
checked against, plus that they do not all name the same ramp — because agreeing
with seven identical values would prove nothing. **9 checks, 0 failures.**

**A discriminator I tried and threw away**, because it is the kind that looks
rigorous and decides nothing: *"the ramp that puts the most non-black colour on
the icon"*. Both candidates score **identically** — all three sub-palettes are
fully populated, so every ramp colours every pixel. Measuring it is what stopped
it going in.

### And a dead index found on the way

`gen4_species_sprites` was **not in `GEN4_PREFIXED`**, so the whole index the
species stage writes was dead data: written on every import, loaded by nothing,
read by nothing. The battle's own front and back pictures reach it by another
route entirely, which is why nobody noticed. It is loaded now because the icons
ride inside it — and the per-species sheet paths, the female variants and the
height offsets are all still sitting in it unused, which is worth a look next
time something needs them.

The icons are published as `data.icons.bySpecies[species] = { image, frameHeight }`
— the shape `Gen3PartyMenu`, `Gen4PartyMenu`, the box, the summary page and the
Poketch's party app all already read, so none of them needed a Gen 4 branch.
A cache that brings its own `icons` still wins, which is the rule every other
lift in `Data.lua` follows.

## The summary page's Pokémon: a slot declared and never filled

`Gen4SummaryMenu` has carried a `picture` entry in its layout since the day it
was written, and nothing had ever drawn into it. Every summary page in Sinnoh
came up as a column of numbers beside an **empty plate** — not a bug that
reports itself, because the screen worked and the words were right and the only
symptom was an absence.

### Where it goes, and this one is stated twice

**STATED.** `PokemonSummaryScreen_LoadMonSprite` (3d_anim.c 338) creates the
sprite at **(52, 104)**, and those two numbers are not a corner:
`PokemonSpriteManager_CreateSpriteAtIndex` assigns its `x` and `y` straight to
`transforms.xCenter` and `transforms.yCenter`. What settles what *that* means is
a different caller entirely — the egg-hatch cutscene creates its sprite at
`(HW_LCD_WIDTH / 2, HW_LCD_HEIGHT / 2 + yOffset)`, which is only the middle of
the screen if the pair is the **centre**.

**MEASURED.** The summary screen is ten tilemaps over one 480-tile sheet
(`pl_pst_gra.narc`), and all ten were composed and measured. Every one of them
carries the same backing plate in the left column:

```
x 20..83   y 72..135      64 square, identical on all ten pages
centre     (51.5, 103.5)
```

A 64-pixel square centred on (52, 104) occupies **exactly** x 20..83 and
y 72..135 — the half-pixel is what an even-sided rect does, it straddles its
centre rather than sitting on it. **Ten pages of art and the cartridge's own
code, agreeing to the pixel.**

The old value in the table was `{ x = 20, y = 70 }` — the plate's top-left
corner, with a two-pixel error in y, and no derivation written beside it. It had
never been wrong in any visible way because nothing had ever read it. The new
entry carries `plate = 64` as well, and that field is what lets the screen tell
the two shapes apart: a cache imported before today still says `{20, 70}` under
the same key, and there is nothing in the *values* to distinguish a corner from
a centre. A record without `plate` is declined and the screen's own constant —
the cartridge's pair — is used instead, so an old cache lands in the right place
rather than eight pixels up and to the left of it.

**The picture is 80 square and the plate is 64**, so a Pokémon overhangs its
plate on every side. That is the cartridge's look and not a sizing mistake: the
sprite is drawn at `MON_AFFINE_SCALE(1)`, 1:1, and allowed to overflow. Shrunk
to fit the plate it would be a different screen.

### ...and it is mirrored

```c
monSprite.flip = SpeciesData_GetFormValue(species, form, SPECIES_DATA_FLIP_SPRITE) ^ 1;
```

The `^ 1` is the whole thing: the summary reverses every species whose flag is
**clear** — 480 of the 508 personal records — and leaves the twenty-eight that
are set alone. The same rule is applied to the mon icon twelve hundred lines
away in `sprites.c`, which is the second statement.

**What the flag is not is a facing**, and the pictures say so outright: Torterra
has it SET and Bulbasaur CLEAR, and both are drawn facing left. So it cannot
mean "this art happens to point the other way".

**What it reads as is "do not reverse this one"**, and the members that settle it
are the ones a mirror would falsify:

> UNOWN, whose sprite is a **letter**; SPINDA, whose spots are the whole point of
> it; the Poliwag line's spiral; Teddiursa's crescent.

That is written down as a *reading* and not a derivation, because the
twenty-eight are not all obvious from outside the art team — Torterra and
Chimchar are in the set and I cannot say why. The consequence is not in doubt
either way: those species come up facing the other way from the rest of the
party, on the cartridge exactly as here.

**The byte was already in the cache.** `Gen4Species.parse` has read it as
`flipSprite` off the top bit of the byte that carries `bodyColor` since the
species stage was written, and nothing had ever read it back — the third piece
of already-extracted dead data this screen has turned up, after
`gen4_species_sprites` itself and the party icons inside it.

**AND THE OBVIOUS SPELLING WOULD HAVE BROKEN KANTO.** `not def.flipSprite` is
true for a Gen 1 species row, which has no such field — so writing the condition
the natural way would have mirrored every Pokémon in Kanto, Johto and Hoenn on
their own summary screens. The mirror is asked for only where the field
*exists*: `def.flipSprite ~= nil and not def.flipSprite`. There is a check line
for exactly that, and it is the one that would have caught it.

### The egg

`pl_otherpoke` files both eggs under **species 0**, so they land in
`gen4_species_sprites.forms` and on no `data.pokemon` row at all — `Party.isEgg`
is asked first and the picture comes from `forms["000_egg_base"]`. No mirror: an
egg has no personal record to read a flag out of.

The Manaphy egg is extracted, under `000_egg_manaphy`, and is deliberately **not
named** by the screen. Nothing in this port marks an egg as Manaphy's yet, so a
constant for it would be a key nothing could ever choose correctly — and
`tools/gen4_summary_check.lua` asserts that no quoted copy of that key appears in
the screen, while the prose above the constant is free to name it.

### tools/gen4_summary_check.lua — 20 checks, 0 failures

Each number is checked the way it was got, which is the only honest way to test
a file where one constant is derived and another is a reading:

* the **centre** is arithmetic on the constants — `x - plate/2 == 20` and
  `x + plate/2 - 1 == 83` — so it fails if *either* statement moves, rather than
  restating the measured numbers beside themselves;
* the **overhang** is checked against the thing it must not overhang into: the
  label column at x = 112, which was measured off the same art for an unrelated
  reason. 52 + 40 = 92, clear by twenty pixels;
* the **egg key** is asserted against `Gen4Otherpoke.key` on the archive's own
  row, so a renamed form row breaks the check instead of silently emptying the
  plate;
* the **mirror** is exercised for all three inputs — flag set, flag clear, and
  no field at all — with a canary that the decision still has two answers,
  because four passing lines say nothing if the function has collapsed to one.

Two of the twenty are there purely because of how this bug happened: the screen
must contain `def.flipSprite` and it must contain `self:drawPicture()`. A slot
nobody filled is not caught by any assertion about what is *in* the slot.

**Verified by looking**, as everything assembled on this screen has been: the
page art composed out of the archive with Bulbasaur, Unown, Torterra and Piplup
placed on it by the rule above. Bulbasaur and Piplup face right, Unown's letter
reads correctly, Torterra faces left — which is what the flag says, and what the
cartridge shows.

## The numbers on a healthbox — and two things this file had wrong

The level and the HP on a Platinum healthbox were the last pieces of the battle
screen still set in the engine's own face: a sixteen-pixel system face squeezed
into a nine-row band, right-aligned because nothing else would fit. Finishing
them started by re-reading what this document already said about them, and
**both of the claims it rested on were false.**

### Correction one: the numbers are not in the parts blob

> *"HealthBox_DrawCurrentHP does not print text at all: it blits
> HEALTHBOX_PART_NUMBERS_LEFT, _NUMBERS_RIGHT and _SLASH out of the parts blob
> (healthbox.c 840-845)."*

Those three parts are at those lines, and that is exactly why the reading looked
safe. Line 840 is not in `HealthBox_DrawCurrentHP` at all — it is inside
`Healthbox_ToggleHPDisplayMode`, which opens with

```c
switch (healthbox->type) {
case HEALTHBOX_TYPE_PLAYER_SLOT_1:
case HEALTHBOX_TYPE_PLAYER_SLOT_2:
    break;
default:
    return;
}
```

so it runs for the two **doubles** boxes and nothing else. `NUMBERS_LEFT` and
`NUMBERS_RIGHT` are the empty number *field* that swaps in where the bar was
when a doubles box toggles to `numberMode`, and the slash beside them is that
field's slash. They are furniture, not glyphs.

**GREPPING FOR A SYMBOL FINDS EVERY PLACE IT IS MENTIONED AND NOT THE PLACE IT
IS USED.** The line numbers were right and the function they were in was never
checked.

### Correction two: only one thing on the box is text

> *"HealthBox_DrawBattlerName, DrawLevelNumber and DrawMaxHP all print with
> FONT_SYSTEM (healthbox.c 1143, 1316, 1355)."*

1143 is `HealthBox_DrawBattlerName` and is correct. 1316 is
`HealthBox_DrawBallCount` and 1355 is `HealthBox_DrawBallsLeftMessage` — **the
Safari Zone's ball counter**, which is not on an ordinary healthbox at all. The
whole of the lettering that is genuinely text is the **nickname**.

### What actually draws a number

```c
FontSpecialChars_DrawBattleScreenText(ctx, value, 3, padding, buf);
```

from `HealthBox_DrawLevelNumber` (1208), `HealthBox_DrawCurrentHP` (1245) and
`HealthBox_DrawMaxHP` (1262). The face is `font_special_chars.NCGR`, member 4 of
`pl_font.narc`: **twenty-three 8×8 tiles, one glyph each** —

```
0..9  the digits      10  "/"      11-12  "Lv."
13-14 "No."           15-16 "ID."  17-22  three unused Lv variants
```

and `sNonNumericWidths` in `font_special_chars.c` states every one of those
offsets outright, in tiles, which is the second reading of the layout.

**AND THE SHEET IS ALREADY IN THE CACHE.** `pl_font.narc` has been walked by the
screens stage since it was written; `font/font_special_chars.png` is sitting
there. What was missing was never the pixels.

### The colours are the caller's, and the background is the box

The tile data is not a picture. Every nibble is 0, 1 or 2 — background,
foreground, shadow — and `FontSpecialChars_Init(fg, shadow, bg)` rewrites them
into real palette indices before the strip is drawn once. The battle asks for
**(14, 2, 15)** at `battle_main.c` 529, and the line straight after it is what
makes this one sheet and not two:

```c
battleSys->specialCharsLevel = battleSys->specialCharsHP;
```

**The level and the HP are the same face in the same colours.**

Measured in the healthbox family's palette (member 71 of `pl_batt_obj.narc`):

```
14  (255, 255, 255)   white          the glyph
 2  ( 41,  49,  41)   dark green     its shadow
15  (107, 115,  90)   panel green    the "background"
```

That third one settles a question that would otherwise have been a guess. **The
background index is the colour the box already is**: rows 39..47 of the
assembled `healthbox_player_singles` are that exact green, flat, all the way
across. So the cartridge is not painting a background on — it is painting the
colour that was already there. The stage writes the strip with a **transparent**
background, which is the same picture on the box and the right one anywhere else
the strip gets used. (It does get used elsewhere: the party screen's HP, the bag,
the shop and the Battle Castle each build their own context off this sheet with
their own three colours. Only the battle's are written, because only the battle
draws from it yet.)

Nine tiles of the twenty-three would have been enough to notice a repack: tiles
0..16 use no nibble above 2, and tiles 17..22 — the three unused Lv variants —
go up to 15. `Gen4SpecialChars.looksRight` tests exactly the first seventeen,
which is the range where "the values are roles" is actually true.

### Where every number sits

Each drawer names a **VRAM byte offset** into the box's own character data, and
the box is two 64×64 OAM squares side by side with tiles 0..63 in the left and
64..127 in the right — which the cell bank established when the boxes were first
assembled. So an offset is a tile and a tile is a position:

```
tile t < 64    ->  ( (t % 8) * 8,       (t // 8) * 8 )
tile t >= 64   ->  ( 64 + (u % 8) * 8,  (u // 8) * 8 )     u = t - 64
```

```
                       Lv block        level digits    cur HP        max HP
player_singles         (88, 16)        (104, 20)       (64, 40)      (96, 40)
enemy                  (72, 16)        ( 88, 20)       —             —
player_doubles         (80, 16)        ( 96, 20)       (64, 32)      (96, 32)
```

**THE LEVEL DIGITS ARE FOUR PIXELS DOWN FROM THEIR TILE, AND THAT IS NOT A
NUDGE.** `HealthBox_DrawLevelNumber` copies each glyph's first 16 bytes into the
*bottom* half of the upper tile and its last 16 into the *top* half of the lower
one, so an eight-row digit straddles the boundary at y = 16 and lands on rows
20..27.

**THREE THINGS CONFIRM THE ARITHMETIC, none of them the arithmetic:**

1. The level digits land at the **right-hand end of the green panel** that was
   measured off the art months ago for the nickname — 104..127 against a panel
   ending at 127 on the solo box, 88..111 against one ending at 111 on the foe's.
2. The current HP (64..87) and the max HP (96..119) leave **exactly one
   eight-pixel column** between them — and the assembled box art has a diagonal
   `/` baked into x 88..95, y 41..46. The slash is *in the picture* because it
   never changes; the numbers are not, because they do. Nothing in the
   calculation knew the slash was there.
3. The HP row lands at y 40..47, inside the **nine-row band** this port had
   already measured, for a different reason, before any of this existed.

### The "Lv" is a picture, and it is gendered

`HealthBox_DrawLevelText` picks `LEVEL_MALE` / `_FEMALE` / `_GENDERLESS` and
copies a TOP pair and a BOTTOM pair out of the parts blob, so the block is 16
wide and 16 tall with the gender symbol baked into it. Gender is asked of
`Pokemon.genderOf` rather than of `mon.gender`, because a Pokémon that has never
been asked carries none and the answer has to come from the species ratio —
which is the trap ATTRACT paid for once already.

### Alignment is the whole of CharCode_FromInt

Every call passes three columns, so the only thing that decides where a number
sits is the padding mode:

```
PADDING_MODE_NONE     a leading zero emits NOTHING   -> short, LEFT-justified
PADDING_MODE_SPACES   a leading zero emits a blank   -> full, RIGHT-justified
```

The current HP is `SPACES` and the max HP is `NONE`, which is why `68/142` sits
hard against the slash on the left and starts immediately after it on the right.
The level is `NONE`, so `Lv5` puts the 5 against the "Lv" block rather than three
columns away from it.

A digit of ten or more emits `CHAR_WIDE_QUESTION`, which is not one of
`CHAR_WIDE_0..9`, and the drawer fills any non-digit with the background — so a
number too wide for its field **loses its leading column** rather than drawing a
glyph the strip does not carry. `numberCells` reproduces that rather than
clamping, because clamping would be a different picture.

### How it degrades, and one move that was not a refactor

`drawHealthboxNumbers` is all-or-nothing and answers whether it drew: a picture
"Lv" beside a system-face number would look worse than either alone. A cache
imported before the digit stage keeps the old path — the system face,
right-aligned in the band — and says so by simply being what it was.

`partsFor` was **moved up** three hundred lines rather than forward-declared when
the "Lv" block started reading it too. A file-local called above its own `local
function` line resolves as a global, gets nil and raises, and this port has now
paid for that twice; moving the definition is the fix that cannot be got wrong
again later.

`tools/gen4_battlescene_check.lua` is **98 checks, 0 failures**, 21 of them new.
The ones that earn their place are the two that re-derive rather than restate:
the level block must fit inside the panel measured off the art, and the two HP
fields must leave exactly one column for a slash nobody told the calculation
about.

**Verified by looking**, composed out of the cartridge: the assembled solo box
with the male "Lv" block, level 47, and 68/142 either side of the baked slash.

## Using a TM in Sinnoh raised — three faults in a row, and the note was one of them

The Gen 4 party-menu alias in `Screens.lua` carried a comment saying that TM
teaching was left unserved "on purpose", because it "needs words this
cartridge's cache does not carry". That was wrong twice over: the cache does
carry them, and what the gap actually cost was not a wrong-looking screen but a
**crash**.

The chain, in the order a player walks into it:

1. `BagMenu.useOn` pushes `PartyMenu` with `{ pickOnly, keepOpen, onSwitch,
   tmhm }` for any item with a `machine` record — on every cartridge, because
   `Gen4BagMenu:choose` calls that same published function.
2. `servedBy` declines the whole push, because the Gen 4 alias lists the first
   three keys and not `tmhm`. **An alias declines on any unlisted key**, so one
   missing name throws away a push that was otherwise fully served.
3. `resolveId` then reaches `if not isGen3(game) then return id, arg end` — a
   Platinum cache is not a Hoenn one — and hands back the **Game Boy** id. This
   is the third time this exact fall-through has cost a screen, after the
   keyboard and the Pokédex.
4. Whichever screen serves it eventually calls `ItemEffects.use`, which asks
   `for _, m in ipairs(speciesDef.tmhm)`. **A Gen 4 cache has no `tmhm` on any
   species.** `ipairs(nil)` raises.

So the visible symptom would have been the game ending, not Kanto's party list.

### The list the cartridge does not store

`def.tmhm` — a plain list of move ids — is what `ItemEffects.use` scans, what
`DayCare` reads for egg moves, and what a party screen asks to print ABLE or
UNABLE beside a member. The Gen 1–3 extractors write it directly. The Gen 4 one
never did, because **the cartridge has no such list**. It has a 128-bit mask:
four `u32` on every personal record, which `Gen4Species.parse` has read as
`tmLearnset` since the species stage was written and nothing ever read back.

`CanPokemonFormLearnTM` turns a machine id into a word and a bit:

```c
if (tmID < 32)      { tmFlag = 1 << tmID;        mask 1 }
else if (tmID < 64) { tmFlag = 1 << (tmID - 32); mask 2 }
else if (tmID < 96) { tmFlag = 1 << (tmID - 64); mask 3 }
else                { tmFlag = 1 << (tmID - 96); mask 4 }
```

so bit *b* of word *w* is machine `w * 32 + b`, **zero-based**, in the same
TM01..TM92, HM01..HM08 order `sTMHMMoves` is in — which is what makes the
pairing one index rather than a join.

**TWO THINGS SAY THE BIT ORDER IS RIGHT, AND NEITHER IS THE ARITHMETIC:**

* 100 machines live in 128 bits, so 28 bits are spare — and they are spare in
  the cartridge too. Measured over all 493 species: the highest bit set
  anywhere is **99**, and **nothing is set at or above 100**. A wrong word
  order or a flipped bit order scatters set bits into that empty tail.
* **MAGIKARP AND DITTO COME OUT WITH EXACTLY ZERO.** They are the two species
  in the game that learn no machine at all, and "exactly none" is not a result
  a wrong reading produces — a wrong reading produces a plausible handful.

And the positive control, for the same reason: Bulbasaur comes out with 28,
ending HM01 Cut, HM04 Strength, HM06 Rock Smash; Pikachu with 32, including
TM24 Thunderbolt, TM25 Thunder and TM73 Thunder Wave. Across the whole file,
508 records and **18,043 machine entries**.

### The words were there all along — bank 453

`generated/text_banks.txt` lists `TEXT_BANK_PARTY_MENU` on line 454, and that
file's zero-based line numbers are the cartridge's bank ids — the rule every
other bank in this port was taken from. Confirmed against the cartridge rather
than against the list: bank 453 decodes to **205 entries**, exactly the count
in `res/text/party_menu.json`, and entry for entry.

```
 33 "Teach which Pokémon?"      145 "SWITCH"        154 "ENTER"
169..174  FIRST SECOND THIRD FOURTH FIFTH SIXTH
175 "ABLE!"   176 "UNABLE!"     177 "LEARNED"       200 "CONFIRM"
```

**PLATINUM SAYS "UNABLE!", NOT "NOT ABLE".** Emerald's word is NOT ABLE and Gen
1's is too, so a screen reusing either would show a word this cartridge does not
use, with an exclamation mark missing from the other two. That is the kind of
seam this port does not leave — and it is exactly what the old note claimed was
the *reason* not to serve the screen at all.

The panel answers the question instead of showing the numbers while a machine
is open, which is what the cartridge does: what is being chosen is whether this
Pokémon can learn the move, and its current HP has nothing to do with that.
**The bar stays** — it is the only thing left saying which of them is hurt, and
a player picking a target still wants to know. The question goes along the
bottom strip, right-aligned and cut to whatever CANCEL leaves, because the face
is proportional and a whole sentence placed at a fixed column runs through
CANCEL on exactly the wordings long enough to matter.

### What is still declined, and now for a true reason

`chooseOrder` and `onOrder` stay out of the alias. The old note said they needed
words; they do not — 154 ENTER, 155 NO ENTRY and 169..174 are extracted and
sitting in the record. The real reason is that **the only caller in the port
that pushes them is `Gen3Commands.chooseParty`, a Gen 3 script special.** No
Platinum cache ever sends one, so listing them would serve a push that never
arrives. The day a Gen 4 command needs it, only the screen has to be written.

### tools/gen4_party_check.lua — 18 checks, 0 failures

Three separate things fail in three different ways here — the alias (wrong
screen), the list (a crash), the words (Emerald's English) — so each is checked
on its own terms.

The alias check pushes **the exact four-key table `BagMenu.useOn` builds**, not
a reduced one: `servedBy` declines on any unlisted key, so a check that pushed
`{tmhm=...}` alone would pass while the real push still fell to Kanto. It is
run against the un-fixed alias to prove it fails, which is the only real proof
a check works. Beside it sit the plain field push and the in-battle push, so a
change cannot fix one by breaking another, and a **canary**: the team-order
push must still be declined, because an alias that served everything would pass
all three and be a different bug.

The machine-list check re-derives the lists from the mask, written from
`CanPokemonFormLearnTM` rather than copied from the extractor — and what makes
that a check rather than a second copy of the same mistake is that its *output*
is asserted against species facts nobody's code chose: Magikarp and Ditto at
zero, Bulbasaur's three HMs, the empty 28-bit tail. Stored lists are compared
against derived ones where they exist; a cache written before this stage is
**reported, not failed**, because that is the state every cache was in.

`ItemEffects` also gained an `or {}` on that scan. The fallback answer is
"cannot learn", which is the safe half of the two: a machine that refuses is a
stale cache, while a machine that teaches off an empty list would be teaching
anything to anything.

## A check that had been grading a file outside the tree

Lowering one opcode is what caught it. `openpokemonnamingscreen` went in;
`tools/gen4_coverage_check.lua` moved from 76,027 lowered instructions to
76,032, and `tools/gen4_seam_check.lua` printed **byte-identical output** —
same 84,519 rows, same 150 distinct verbs. Two tools reading the same corpus
cannot disagree about whether a lowering exists unless they are reading
different files.

The seam check opened with this:

```lua
package.path = "/mnt/user-data/uploads/.../?.lua;/tmp/g4/?.lua;"
             .. "/tmp/g4/src/import/?.lua;" .. package.path
```

and a hard-coded ROM path beside it. Three absolutes from the machine it was
written on, **prepended**, so `require` found whatever sat at those paths before
it ever looked at the tree the tool was run from. On any other machine the check
could not run at all; on the one it was written on, it silently graded a
snapshot.

**THIS IS THE SECOND TIME.** `tools/gen4_command_audit.lua` was caught for
exactly this — "43 checks, 0 failures" measured against a copy of
`Gen4Commands` from before that session's edits — and fixed by self-locating
from `arg[0]`. The fix was never carried across. And it was only half a fix
anyway: **locating the tree does not prove the module that loaded came from
it.**

So the seam check now carries the canary that would have caught both:

```lua
local loadedFrom = (debug.getinfo(VM.lower, "S").source or ""):gsub("^@", "")
local beside = root .. "../src/script/Gen4ScriptVM.lua"
-- compare the BYTES, not the paths
```

A path comparison would not do — two paths can spell the same file, and two
different files can both end in the right name. Run from a tree whose
`src/script/` holds a different lowering, it stops with

```
!! the lowering that loaded is NOT the one beside this tool:
     loaded: ./src/script/Gen4ScriptVM.lua
     beside: /tmp/canary/tools/../src/script/Gen4ScriptVM.lua
   nothing below would be measuring the tree.
```

which is the only proof a check of this kind can offer about itself.

Fixing the paths broke it a second way, and that is worth recording too. The
three loaders were required by **bare name** — `require("NdsRom")` — which does
not begin with `src.` and so slipped past the module shim entirely, resolving
through the `/tmp/g4/src/import/?.lua` entry. Requiring them properly meant the
shim started answering for them, and an inert stub's `NdsRom.open` returns
nothing at all — an `assert` with no arguments. The tangle held itself up.

With the tool reading the tree: **84,519 rows, 151 distinct verbs, 151 have a
handler, 0 do not.**

## The nickname prompt, and a better way to rank what is left

`openpokemonnamingscreen` was unlowered at every one of its five sites:
**Sandgem Town**, Eterna City's Name Rater, the Mining Museum's fossil,
Hearthome and Veilstone. Sandgem is the second town, so every gift Pokémon in
Sinnoh was handed over without ever being offered a name.

The operand order is slot then destination, which `ScrCmd_OpenPokemonNamingScreen`
states — `ScriptContext_GetVar` first, then `ScriptContext_GetVarPointer` — and
the call sites agree without being asked to: three of the five compute the slot
as `getpartycount` then `subvar 1`, the member just handed over.

**WHAT THE DESTINATION MEANS IS THE OPPOSITE OF THE GUESS:**

```c
if (String_Compare(textInputStr, startingName) == 0) returnCode = 1;
if (returnCode == 0) sub_0203DF68(taskMan);   // <- this is what writes the name
if (dest != NULL) *dest = returnCode;
```

`returnCode` is **zero when the name changed** and **one when it did not**, and
one is also the answer for backing out. Every call site compares against 1 and
skips its follow-up line — `comparevartovalue 0x800C 1` then `callif` the "it is
now called X" message. Defaulting to 0 would make all five announce a rename
that never happened, so the command writes 1 first and overwrites it only on the
branch that actually renamed.

### tools/gen4_map_reach.lua — where the tail is, not how big it is

The coverage check ranks the unlowered tail by **occurrence**, and that ranking
is dominated by one room: `callbattletowerfunction` ×146, one building behind
one door nobody has to open. A player walking from Twinleaf to the Elite Four
never meets it.

Ranking by **how many maps an opcode reaches** produces a different order, and
it is the order worth working through:

```
initturnbackcave           20 maps   Turnback Cave
playelevatoranimation       7 maps   Hearthome, Jubilife TV, Resort Area, Veilstone Store, Vista Lighthouse
getfloorsabove              6 maps   (the same lifts)
finishnpctrade              4 maps   Eterna City, OREBURGH CITY, Route 226, Snowpoint City
initnpctrade                4 maps   (the same four)
startnpctrade               4 maps   (the same four)
getnpctraderequestedspecies 4 maps   (the same four)
openpartymenufortrade       4 maps   (the same four)
activateroamingpokemon      3 maps   Eterna City, Fullmoon Island, Verity Cavern
bufferfloornumber           3 maps   Jubilife TV, Resort Area, Veilstone Store
```

`finishnpctrade` occurs eleven times — far down the occurrence list — and sits
on four maps, one of which is **Oreburgh City, the third town**. An occurrence
count says "rare"; a map count says "on the road". **The in-game trades are the
largest main-path gap left**, and the department-store lifts are the second.

593 maps walked, **114 have at least one unlowered instruction** (117 before the
nickname prompt went in). The tool also prints the list the other way round —
maps worst first, with the opcodes each is missing — which is the list to read
when a player says a scene did nothing.

It is deliberately **not** a pass/fail check: the tail is work that has not been
done, and a number that only goes down is not something to assert. It prints;
the checks assert. It carries the same module canary as the seam check, because
a report that cannot say which tree it read is worth no more than a check that
cannot.

## The four in-game trades, which did nothing at all

`tools/gen4_map_reach.lua` put them at the top of its list the moment it
existed: five commands, four maps, and the first of those maps is **Oreburgh
City — the third town**. Ranked by occurrence they are invisible;
`finishnpctrade` occurs eleven times in the whole cartridge.

### The record reads as itself

`/fielddata/pokemon_trade/fld_trade.narc`, one member per trade, and the member
is **twenty `u32` in a row** — `struct NPCTradeMon`, all words and no packing,
so nothing about the layout can be got wrong except the field *order*:

```
species hpIV atkIV defIV speedIV spAtkIV spDefIV unused1 otID
cool beauty cute smart tough personality heldItem otGender unused2
language requestedSpecies
```

Four members, each exactly 80 bytes, and the species/requested pairs come out
as Platinum's own four trades:

```
0  ABRA      (63)  "Kazza"   of Hilary   for a MACHOP   (66)
1  CHATOT   (441)  "Charap"  of Norton   for a BUIZEL  (418)
2  HAUNTER   (93)  "Gaspar"  of Mindy    for a MEDICHAM (308)
3  MAGIKARP (129)  "Foppa"   of Meister  for a FINNEON  (456)
```

**A WRONG FIELD ORDER DOES NOT PRODUCE THAT.** It produces four plausible
numbers. And the scripts agree without being asked: the four sites pass
`initnpctrade 0/1/2/3` on exactly those four maps, in that order — Oreburgh,
Eterna, Snowpoint, Route 226. Two unrelated readings of the same pairing.

The names are bank 370, and the offset between the two halves is the trade
*count* rather than a second table — `NPCTrade_GetOTName` is one line,
`NPCTrade_GetNickname(heapID, MAX_NPC_TRADES + npcTradeID)`:

```
0 Kazza   1 Charap  2 Gaspar  3 Foppa      <- the Pokémon's nicknames
4 Hilary  5 Norton  6 Mindy   7 Meister    <- the trainers who owned them
```

### The script's shape says what each command must do

All four maps run the same block:

```
initnpctrade <id>
setvarfromvar 0x8004, 0x800C        <- the slot the party menu returned
getpartymonspecies 0x8004, 0x8005
getnpctraderequestedspecies 0x800C
comparevartovar 0x8005, 0x800C
gotoif NE <"that is not what I asked for">
startnpctrade 0x8004
finishnpctrade
setflag <this trade's>
```

So **the only thing deciding whether the swap happens is a comparison of two
species numbers** — which means `getnpctraderequestedspecies` leaving its var
unwritten does not merely fail to ask, it makes the branch read whatever the
last comparison left behind. An unlowered var-writing command is the dangerous
kind, and that is now the fifth time this document has had to say so.

### What the Pokémon is

From `NPCTrade_CreateMon`, and one of these is worth knowing before anyone
"fixes" it:

* **Its level is the level of the one you gave.** The record has no level field
  at all; `level` is read off the party member being traded away. Every trade
  is an even swap in levels, which is why these four are worth doing at any
  point in the game.
* The nickname and OT name are bank 370's, and `hasNickname` is TRUE.
* The six IVs, held item, OT id, OT gender and language are the record's; the
  five contest stats are extracted and not modelled.
* `GF_ASSERT(!Pokemon_IsShiny(mon))` — the personality/OT-id pairs are chosen
  so **none of the four can be shiny**.

**The IVs land because of a fix made months ago for a different reason.**
`Data.lua` normalises a Gen 4 species record onto the Gen 3 stat model — it
fills `evYield` from `evYields`, which is the presence test `Stats.isGen3`
makes — so a Gen 4 Pokémon carries `ivs` at 0..31 and the record's six are in
the same range. Without that they would have been DVs at 0..15 and these would
be nonsense. The check asserts all 24 fall inside 0..31, which is what would
catch an OT id or a personality sliding into an IV slot.

### What is not built, said out loud

`FieldTask_StartNPCTrade` plays the **trade cutscene**. There is no trade
animation anywhere in this port, so the swap happens and the scene does not.
That is stated in the command rather than left to be noticed — the alternative
was what was happening before, which is a trade that silently does nothing.

`getselectedpartyslot` also stops being a stub. It answered CANCELLED
unconditionally "because the menus in front of it are not built"; the trade's
party menu is one of them, so it now reads `ctx.g4PartySlot` **when that is
set** and keeps the honest CANCELLED when it is not. Nothing that used to
answer NONE stops doing so.

### Numbers

`gen4_party_check.lua` is **31 checks, 0 failures** with the trades extracted
(28 against a cache that predates the stage, which it *reports* rather than
fails). Corpus coverage 76,032 → **76,071 lowered, 97.41%**; the seam check
reads **156 distinct verbs, 156 with handlers**.

Thirty-nine instructions out of 78,093 is five hundredths of a percent and four
whole conversations that did nothing. **The percentage is still not the measure
of anything a player meets.**

## Every lift in Sinnoh opened onto nothing, because of two comments

`gen4_map_reach.lua` put `playelevatoranimation` (7 maps) and `getfloorsabove`
(6 maps) at the top of what was left on the main path, so I went looking for a
missing feature. There was no missing feature. There were **two notes in this
port that stated something settled, and both of them were wrong about the same
save slot.**

### The first note: "a `nowhere` sentinel"

`Gen4Events.lua` said, of the warp block:

> 1,207 of 1,213 have a destination below 593 … the other six are 4095, a
> `nowhere` sentinel.

4095 is `0xfff`, and `field_control.c` 1011 is the only place the cartridge ever
looks at it:

```c
if (warpEvent->destWarpID == 0x100) {
    GF_ASSERT(warpEvent->destHeaderID == 0xfff);
    *nextMap = *(FieldOverworldState_GetSpecialLocation(...));
}
```

It is not nowhere. It is **the dynamic destination** — the same idea as Gen 3's
`MAP_G127_N127`, which this port has resolved through `save.gen3DynamicWarp`
since the truck a new game starts inside. The pair is what identifies it, and
the pair is what the extractor was throwing away: the header alone is a number
and the anchor alone is a number, but `0xfff` with `0x100` is the exact thing
pret asserts.

Measured, and it is not six warps scattered about the region — **all six are
warp 1, at (3, 6), with anchor 256**, and the six maps are the six lift cars:

| car | building | header |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C01R0208 | Jubilife TV | 18 |
| C05R0103 | Hearthome City, south-east house | 105 |
| C05R0803 | Hearthome City, north-east house | 114 |
| C07R0206 | Veilstone department store | 142 |
| T07R0103 | Resort Area, Ribbon Syndicate | 463 |
| C08R0802 | Vista Lighthouse | 516 |

Six identical warps in six lift cars is not a coincidence and it is not
"nowhere".

### The second note: "it stamps the MET LOCATION"

`Gen4ScriptVM.lua` lowered `setspeciallocation` to a **no-op**, with:

```lua
-- `setspeciallocation` takes five operands and writes none; it stamps the MET
-- LOCATION on what you catch in the marsh.
```

The slot has four readers in the cartridge and the met location is not one of
them:

| reader | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `field_control.c` 1011 | the lift cars' dynamic warp |
| `encounter.c` 484 | the Great Marsh, when the balls run out |
| `field_map_change.c` 1084 | coming back up from the Underground |
| `unk_02049D08.c` 228 | the Battle Tower's communication club |

So the lift scripts were writing a floor into a command that discarded it, and
the door they then walked you into had nothing to resolve. **Put the two notes
together and every lift in the region was a dead end** — Jubilife TV's four
floors, the Veilstone department store's six, both Hearthome houses, the Ribbon
Syndicate and the Vista Lighthouse. Neither comment was a guess someone left a
`TODO` on. Both were written as fact.

That is the third time in this document a *prose note* has been the fault rather
than the code under it, and the rule stays where it was put: **when a comment
and its code agree with each other and disagree with the cartridge, they are
both wrong together.**

### The operand that was not an x

`Location` (include/location.h) is five fields, and the order is not the one the
operand names suggest:

```
mapHeaderID, warpId, x, z, faceDirection
```

so `setspeciallocation 14 1 18 2 1` is header 14, **warp 1**, then (18, 2) and
facing south. Reading operand 2 as an x is the obvious mistake and it would have
been invisible, because the *third* and *fourth* operands really are coordinates
and they really are near the right tile. What settles it is `field_map_change.c`
226:

```c
if (location->warpId != WARP_ID_NONE) {
    warpEvent = MapHeaderData_GetWarpEventByIndex(fieldSystem, location->warpId);
    location->x = warpEvent->x;
    location->z = warpEvent->z;
}
```

— the warp index **overwrites** the coordinates, and the map-connection path
hands the change `(headerID, warpId, 0, 0, dir)` with the coordinates zeroed
anyway.

And there is a check for it that no table here decides. Take every
`(mapHeaderID, warpId)` pair the cartridge's scripts write — a walk over
`scr_seq.narc` finds thirteen distinct ones — resolve each against the cache's
own warp lists, and ask **where the resolved warp goes**:

```
header 11   warp 2 -> C01R0201 (18,3) -> C01R0208    Jubilife TV 1F  -> its car
header 12   warp 3 -> C01R0202 (18,2) -> C01R0208
header 13   warp 4 -> C01R0203 (18,2) -> C01R0208
header 14   warp 1 -> C01R0204 (18,2) -> C01R0208
header 137  warp 2 -> C07R0201 (15,2) -> C07R0206    Veilstone 1F    -> its car
header 138  warp 2 -> C07R0202 (15,2) -> C07R0206
header 139  warp 2 -> C07R0203 (15,2) -> C07R0206
header 140  warp 2 -> C07R0204 (15,2) -> C07R0206
header 141  warp 1 -> C07R0205 (15,2) -> C07R0206
header 566  warp 1 -> C07R0207 (14,2) -> C07R0206    and its basement
header 461  warp 1 -> T07R0101 (5,2)  -> T07R0103    Ribbon Syndicate
header 462  warp 0 -> T07R0102 (5,2)  -> T07R0103
header 125  warp 2 -> C06R0101 (5,2)  -> D06R0206    Pastoria gate -> the Marsh
```

**Thirteen for thirteen, each one landing on the door into its own lift car.**
Read as an x, the operand cannot do that. This is the check worth having,
because it proves the *reading* rather than restating it.

The last row is the Great Marsh, and it is the grain of truth in the note that
was wrong: the Pastoria gate stores its own marsh doorway, which is where
running out of balls puts you back. That is a destination, not a met location.

### The lift remembers the floor you got on at

`field_map_change.c` 232, in the same function, on arrival:

```c
if (warpEvent->destWarpID == 0x100) {
    *specialLocation = *entranceLocation;
}
```

**Stepping into a car overwrites the slot with the door you just left.** Which
is the whole of how three of the six lifts work: Hearthome's two cars and the
Vista Lighthouse's have no panel and no receptionist at all. Their entire script
is

```
GetFloorsAbove VAR_ELEVATOR_FLOORS_ABOVE
GoToIfEq 1, <up>
GoToIfEq 0, <down>
```

— they ask about the *special location*, which is the floor you boarded at, and
warp you to the other one. Without the entrance capture they would answer about
whichever floor some other lift was last sent to, and on a fresh save about
nothing. It is also what makes walking straight back out of any car return you
to the floor you came from instead of wherever you last went.

This is why `Warp.noteGen4Entrance` is called from `OverworldState:takeWarp`
rather than from the resolver: the cartridge loads a header and then asks which
warp it arrived at, and this port resolves a destination — so the map being left
is only known at the door.

### FieldMenu_GetFloorsAbove is a switch

Eighteen cases over header ids with a default of 1, so there is nothing in the
cartridge's *data* to extract and `Gen4Elevators.FLOORS_ABOVE` is transcribed.
What makes a transcription checkable is that all eighteen ids were resolved
against the cache's own headers and every one landed on the building it names —
**18/18**, including the three that would have caught a wrong list:

* Veilstone's B1F is **566**, four hundred ids away from its own building;
* the Ribbon Syndicate's pair sit at **461/462**, not beside the Veilstone run;
* the Vista Lighthouse's lower floor is **Sunyshore City itself** (150), because
  that lift's ground floor is outdoors.

And the scripts agree independently: the Jubilife lift's own
`setspeciallocation 11 / 12 / 13 / 14` names those four ids outright.

The default is **1, not 0**, and that matters more than a default usually does —
`above == 1` is exactly Hearthome's "go up" branch, so an unrecognised floor
still moves the car instead of jamming it.

### "0F" would have been the giveaway

`bufferfloornumber`'s second operand is not a signed floor number:

```c
GF_ASSERT(floor <= 5);
if (floor == 0) floor = MenuEntries_Text_B1F;
else            floor += MenuEntries_Text_1F - 1;
```

**Zero is the basement.** The Veilstone store buffers `5 4 3 2 1 0`, which is
5F down to B1F — its six floors exactly — and formatting the operand as a number
would have printed the basement as "0F". The labels are cartridge text, not
literals: bank **361** (the menu-entries bank; `generated/text_banks.txt` line
362, the same zero-based-line rule that puts the party menu at 453), entries
116 "1F" through 120 "5F" and 121 "B1F". Read back out of the ROM to be sure the
offset was right, and the neighbours line up — 114 "TOUGH CONTEST", 123
"LOOKOUT".

### The one pointer operand that is an input

`showcurrentfloor` takes a var *pointer*, and `gen4_operand_roles.py` duly
flagged it as a dropped destination — which is the check doing its job and
being wrong for the first time in its life. The var is a **handle**:

```c
static void CurrentFloorWindowSystaskCallback(...) {
    if (*menuManager->selectedOptionPtr == 0xffff) { ...close the window... }
}
```

The window watches it; the **script** writes it, three rows later, with
`setvar VAR_ELEVATOR_FLOORS_ABOVE, -1`. So a lowering that "fixed" the warning
by writing a zero would clobber the floor count the panel is about to branch on
— the exact failure the roles check exists to prevent, introduced by satisfying
it. It is listed in a new `IN_OUT_HANDLES` table *with the reason*, so a second
command in that shape has to be argued for on the same page rather than added
to a silent skip list.

### What is honestly not there

Two rows are no-ops and say which they are:

* **`playelevatoranimation`** — the car rocking. There is no elevator cutscene
  in this port and one is not faked; the lift takes you to the floor, it just
  arrives without the ride.
* **`showcurrentfloor`** — the "Current Floor / 3F" window in the corner. A HUD
  this port does not draw, the same call this file already makes for the money
  box. Nothing is lost by it that is not recoverable: the string it would
  interpolate is filled by `bufferfloornumber` whether anything draws it or not.

`checkisdepartmentstoreregular` is the interesting one, because the honest
lowering is *not* "no". It reads
`VAR_DEPARTMENT_STORE_REGULAR_COUNTER` (0x4042, by the same enum walk over
`generated/vars_flags.txt` that put `VAR_PLAYER_STARTER` at 0x4030 — checked
twice against the scripts, which name `VAR_ELEVATOR_FLOORS_ABOVE` at 0x40CE and
`VAR_RESULT` at 0x800C with exactly the ids the walk produces) and compares it
against five. The counter is incremented by the shop, once per purchase at one
of the nine Veilstone counters, and this port still declines those counters
because their stock lists are a second table the cache does not carry. So today
it answers no — **which is also what the cartridge tells a player who has bought
nothing** — and it starts working on its own the day the stock lists land,
without this command changing.

### Numbers

`gen4_lift_check.lua` is new: **37 checks, 0 failures**, and seven of them are
Gold/Crystal/Prism regressions, because both edits live in shared code
(`Warp.lua`, `OverworldController.lua`) and the cheapest way for this work to
break the older games is for the new arm to catch a door it has no business

Corpus coverage 76,071 → **76,165 lowered, 97.53%**; the seam check reads

Ninety-four instructions out of 78,093 is a tenth of a percent and **six

## The Pokémon League's rising platforms, and a no-op that had argued a third of itself

The last main-path row on the map-reach list was one opcode:

    checkplatformliftnotusedwhenenteredmap   5 maps   POKÉMON LEAGUE

It sits in front of the **platform lifts** — not the department-store lifts from
the section above but a different mechanism entirely: a 3x2 slab that rises
between two heights in the room it is already in. There are **nine**, three on
Iron Island and six in the Pokémon League.

### The note was right about three of them and decided all nine

`Gen4ScriptVM.lua` already lowered `triggerplatformlift` to a no-op, and the
argument was a good one — it dumped Iron Island's B1F-right, B2F-left and B3F
cell by cell, found each room's two "components" were the room plus the map's
unused surround, and concluded the lift was scenery rather than a gate. It even
carried the right lesson: *"a component count is not a measurement; what the
components CONTAIN is."*

And then it covered the six Pokémon League rooms without looking at one of them.
That is the department-store lifts' mistake with the polarity reversed: not a
comment that was wrong, a comment that was **silent about the rest of what it
decided**. Aaron, Bertha, Flint, Lucian, Cynthia's elevator and the Champion's
room were riding on a paragraph about a cave on the other side of the region.

So I measured them. Each League room is a **shaft**: a warp in the wall at the
top (behaviour `0x6E`) and a warp on the floor at the bottom. The question is
whether the column between them is walkable without the platform.

| room | | column | open |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| C10R0102 | the elevator to Aaron | x=4, y 3..15 | 13/13 |
| C10R0104 | the elevator to Bertha | x=4, y 3..15 | 13/13 |
| C10R0106 | the elevator to Flint | x=4, y 3..15 | 13/13 |
| C10R0108 | the elevator to Lucian | x=4, y 3..15 | 13/13 |
| C10R0110 | the elevator to Cynthia | x=4, y 3..23 | 21/21 |
| C10R0111 | the Champion's room | x=8, y 3..18 | 16/16 |

Every tile behaviour 0, no collision bit, in the same ten bits `Map.blockArray`
hands the engine. **The Elite Four are reachable in order without the lift**, and
Cynthia's room ends in an explicit `Warp` to the Hall of Fame hallway rather than
in the platform. The no-op was right for all nine; it is now right *for a reason*
on all nine, and the reason is a check rather than a paragraph.

### The question the slot is asked is answerable

`checkplatformliftnotusedwhenenteredmap <destVar>` is a **var-writer**, which is
the fifth time this document has had to say that an unlowered one is the
dangerous kind. All five sites are the same four lines:

```
SetVar VAR_MAP_LOCAL_0x00, 0
InitPersistedMapFeaturesForPlatformLift
CheckPlatformLiftNotUsedWhenEnteredMap VAR_MAP_LOCAL_0x01
GoToIfEq VAR_MAP_LOCAL_0x01, FALSE, <DisablePlatformLift>    ; sets 0x00 = 1
```

and `VAR_MAP_LOCAL_0x00` is the condition on the room's own coord event — which
this port honours, since `Gen4ScriptVM.bind` carries `var`/`value` through.

The answer is **"did you come in at the bottom"**.
`PersistedMapFeatures_InitForPlatformLift` sets the flag TRUE and then clears it
in the **six League cases only**, and only when the arrival z is not the room's
bottom-floor warp z. The three Iron Island cases set `floorID` from z the same
way and never touch the flag, so **Iron Island answers TRUE on both floors**.
That asymmetry is the whole rule and it is exactly the sort of thing a
transcription reads past, so the check asserts both halves separately — 6/6 and
3/3.

Nine `#define ..._BOTTOM_FLOOR_WARP_Z` constants, and all nine are the y of a
real warp on the map they name. The one that settles the **coordinate space** is
Iron Island B2F-left, whose constant is written `MAP_TILES_COUNT_Z * 1 + 16`:
that is 48, on a 64x64 map, and only a matrix coordinate can be 48 there. The
cache's warp sits at y 48. So the comparison is against the player's matrix y,
and the command uses `toMatrix` — all nine of these maps happen to sit at origin
(0,0), so this is the difference between being right and being accidentally
right.

### Said plainly: nothing a player sees changes

The trigger this var gates is the no-op above, so lowering it moves nothing on
screen today. It is worth doing for two reasons and neither of them is a fix: the
var stops holding the previous comparison, and the persisted slot becomes
truthful for whoever builds the height feature. **Writing that down as "the
Pokémon League now works" would have been the third wrong note in this file's
history**, so it is written down as what it is.

### The start tiles check themselves

`sPerMapPlatformLiftConfiguration` is a C table, so its nine `startTileX/Z` pairs
are transcribed — and a transcription is only worth having if something can
disagree with it. A 3x2 slab from each corner **has to contain that room's own
lift trigger**, and eight of the nine do. The ninth is asserted to have *no*
trigger rather than waved through as an exception: the Champion's room lift is
started by the script after Cynthia, not by walking onto it.

What is *not* copied across: `floorHeights` and `preventGoingDown`. Those are
height data with nothing in this port to check them against, so they are named —
they are in pret's `src/platform_lift.c` — and left there. Copying unverifiable
numbers into a module is how a file acquires its next wrong comment.

### The two coverage floors are not the same number twice

Raising them together failed immediately, and the reason is worth keeping: the
percentage the check *prints* is rounded and the one it *compares* is not.
76,170 / 78,093 is **97.5381%**, which prints as "97.54" and is below a 97.54
floor. The instruction count is exact, so that is the floor to raise; the
percentage moves only when its unrounded value clears the next step. The note is
now in the tool.

### Numbers

`gen4_lift_check.lua` grows from 37 to **50 checks, 0 failures** — the platform
lifts join the department-store lifts in one file because they are the same
subject, and a second lift check would be the first place the two drifted. Proved
to fail: a transposed bottom-floor z, a moved start tile and a dropped
League/Iron-Island asymmetry give four failures, including the asymmetry one,
which is the only fault here a careful reader would plausibly ship.

Corpus 76,165 → **76,170 lowered, 97.54%**; the seam check reads **161 verbs, 161
handlers**; `gen4_operand_roles.py` parses 337 lowerings with **zero dropped
destinations**; the use-before-local scanner reads 209 files, 0 sites.

The gap list is down to **100 maps**, and the Pokémon League is off it. The top
main-path row is now `activateroamingpokemon` — 3 maps, Eterna City, Fullmoon
Island and Verity Cavern — and everything above it by map reach is Battle
Frontier and Battle Tower save-and-link plumbing behind one door.

## Sinnoh's six roamers, and two rules I wrote backwards before reading the file

`activateroamingpokemon` was the top main-path row left: three maps, eight
instructions. Eterna City's south house releases the three Kanto birds once the
National Dex is in, Fullmoon Island releases Cresselia, and **Verity Cavern
releases Mesprit** — which happens the moment the player looks into Lake Verity's
water, early and unmissable. Unlowered, the command that *releases* a roamer did
nothing, so nothing was ever loose and every rule behind it had nothing to act
on.

### The port already had two roamer systems and Platinum matched neither

That is the actual hazard here, and it is not a missing feature — it is a
plausible one. `src/world/RoamMons.lua` is Johto's three beasts and
`src/world/Gen3Roamers.lua` is Hoenn's one, both well built, both with the same
*shape* as what Sinnoh needs. Reusing either would have compiled, run, and been
wrong:

| | Gen 2 | Gen 3 | **Gen 4** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| slots | 3 | 1 | **6** |
| meeting it | 75/256, then 1 of 3 slots | 1 in 4 | **1 in 2** |
| moving | every map load | every map load | **map connection only** |
| graph | none | 20 nodes | **29 nodes, not symmetric** |
| long hop | never | 1 load in 16 | 1 move in 16 |
| avoids | nothing | the map 3 loads ago | the map you just came from |
| after any wild | — | — | **30% they all leave** |

**The odds row is the one worth staring at.** Gen 2 rolls a *slot* and only then
asks where that one is, so three beasts on your route are no likelier than one.
`TryEncounterRoamer` does it the other way round — it gathers every active roamer
*on your map* and only then spends one flat `LCRNG_RandMod(2)`. With Eterna's
three birds loose on one route that is ½ × ⅓ each; read as Gen 2's rule it would
have been 75/256 × ⅙. **A factor of five, and no crash, no log line, nothing.**

### The two I got wrong

Both were in the after-battle pass, and I wrote the module's comment from memory
before opening `roamer_after_battle.c`. It says the opposite of the code on both
counts:

```c
MoveRoamersOffMap(specialEncounter, fieldSystem->location->mapHeaderID);
// all roamers leave if you encounter one
} else {
    if (LCRNG_RandMod(100) < 30) { // 30% chance for roamers to leave
        MoveRoamersOffMap(...);    // even if you don't encounter one
```

1. **Meeting one does not leave it where you met it.** I had written that a
   Sinnoh roamer "is still where you met it until you cross a map boundary,
   which is why chasing one works at all." It is not: every roamer standing on
   that map takes a long hop, including ones you never saw.
2. **An ordinary wild battle scares them off 30% of the time.** This is not
   guessable from anything. It means grinding encounters on a roamer's route
   drives it away three times in ten — so the way to corner one is to *meet* it,
   not to stand in the grass beside it.

The pass also runs on the way out of *every* wild encounter (`encounter.c` state
4), not just a roamer's, which is why the port's hook sits outside the
`battle.roamer` test rather than inside it.

That is the third time this file has recorded a comment being the fault. This
time it was mine and it was caught before it shipped, by the rule the earlier
ones produced: **read the file before writing the sentence, even when the
sentence feels settled.**

### The graph is not symmetric and must not be tidied

`sNearbyRoutes` is 29 rows of up to five neighbours, and the cartridge's own
comment says what it means: *"Includes adjacent routes as well as routes
connected to adjacent towns"* — so Route 202's five are the two off Sandgem and
all three off Jubilife, not just the two it physically touches.

**Two edges go one way only:**

```
 6 -> 9    Route 205 north lists Route 208 (Eterna City between them)
           and Route 208's row does not list 205 north back
13 -> 6    Route 211 west lists Route 205 north, and 205 north's row
           does not list 211 west back
```

The first is written in pret as a bare `9` rather than `RI_ROUTE_208`, which
makes it the easiest entry in the table to lose. Symmetrising the graph invents
two edges; reading it one direction only drops two. Neither crashes, and either
makes a roamer's movement subtly wrong forever — so the check asserts **exactly
these two asymmetries and no others**, along with 78 directed edges, no
self-loops, full reachability, and the four dead ends (Route 217, Route 221,
Valley Windworks, Fuego Ironworks) whose single exit the movement must not loop
on.

### A reroll-until-allowed is a uniform pick over the allowed set

Both movement functions are `while (TRUE) { pick; if (ok) break; }`. I
transcribed that literally first, with a loop bound — and a bounded reroll has a
tail where it gives up and **leaves the roamer where it was**, which the
cartridge never does. The check caught it immediately: a step that was supposed
to refuse one map returned "stayed put", which satisfied "did not go to the
forbidden map" for entirely the wrong reason.

Filtering the candidates first and picking uniformly from what is left is the
same distribution and terminates by construction. The assertion was tightened to
one statement — *lands on a real neighbour that is not the forbidden map* — plus
a second that **both** legal neighbours are reachable, so a silent stay-put
cannot pass either.

One more detail that only reading gives you: a freshly released roamer's "where
it stands" is **Route 201**, not nowhere. `roamerRouteIndexes` starts zeroed, so
the hop at the end of `ActivateSlot` excludes index 0 whether the roamer was ever
there. Mirrored rather than tidied.

### The 29 places check themselves twice

`RoamingPokemonRoutes` is every numbered route in Sinnoh plus two outdoor
stretches that are not routes at all — Valley Windworks and Fuego Ironworks.
Transcribed, and then checked two independent ways against the cache: the header
id must land on the map the table names, **and** the cartridge's own label for
that map must match the route the enum names. 29/29 both ways. Three rows would
catch a wrong list:

* `ROUTE_220` is header **467** and its internal name is **W220**, not R220 — a
  water route, seventy ids past Route 222's 395.
* `ROUTE_205_NORTH` is 349, not 348; the two halves of Route 205 are not
  adjacent ids.
* the last two are `D02` and `D04`, dungeon-prefixed, because the Windworks and
  the Ironworks are outdoor maps attached to buildings.

And all 29 carry a wild-encounter table, which they have to: a roamer is met
*instead of* an ordinary wild encounter, so a place with no encounters is a place
a roamer could hide in forever.

### Where the hooks went, and the older games

Three call sites, all in shared code:

* **the map change** — `noteMap` always, `moveAll` only on a *connection*.
  `FieldSystem_InitFlagsOnMapChange` moves roamers; `FieldSystem_InitFlagsWarp`
  does not. Backwards, this would move all six several times per Pokémon Centre
  visit — invisible, and it would make a roamer impossible to corner.
* **the encounter roll** — beside Johto's and Hoenn's, and deliberately *without*
  their `onWater` refusal: Gen 2 bars a beast while surfing and Gen 4 does not,
  which is why Routes 218 through 222 are in the roaming table at all.
* **the after-battle pass** — outside the `battle.roamer` test, for the 30%.

Since all three live next to Gold, Crystal, Prism and Emerald's own roamers, the
check reads the source and asserts that **the nearest generation guard above each
call is `isGen4()`** — not merely that an `isGen4()` exists somewhere above,
which would pass for a Gen 4 call that had drifted under a Gen 2 guard. It also
asserts the older arms are still *reached*, because a guard that excluded
everything would pass the first test while silently retiring Johto's beasts.

### Numbers

`gen4_roamer_check.lua` is new: **45 checks, 0 failures**, five of them the
shared-code guards. The probabilistic rules are asserted against a *fed* RNG
rather than a real one — a check on a 1-in-2 rule that rolls for real is a check
that passes most days. Proved to fail: symmetrising one edge, dropping a bird's
level to 50, moving a start tile and changing 30 to 31 produce nine failures.

Corpus 76,170 → **76,178 lowered, 97.55%**; the seam check reads **162 verbs, 162
handlers**; `gen4_operand_roles.py` parses 338 lowerings with zero dropped
destinations; the use-before-local scanner reads 212 files, 0 sites.

The gap list is **99 maps**. Everything now above `initturnbackcave` by map reach
is Battle Frontier and Battle Tower save-and-link plumbing behind one door.

## The battle field, the type chart, and the move grid

Three reports from play, one sitting behind each of them, and the third is the
one worth reading twice because the file it was in was already *correct*.

> *"the locations of the land the pokemon are on in battle still arent right
> moves dont seem to be decoded and working properly scratch doesnt work and
> doesnt show a move animation or fx, also for the selection of moves up down
> left right dont work for selection seems to move right when i press down"*

### 1. Both platforms were parked off-screen, and the counter said so

`Gen4Battle.platformAt(side, step)` takes steps **elapsed**: step 0 is the
off-screen start from `sTerrainSpriteTemplates`, step 34 is the settled position
`battle_display.c` sets. That is what its name promises and what
`gen4_battlescene_check.lua` has asserted since the platforms went in.

`BattleState.introSlide` is frames **remaining**. `startBattle` sets it to
`Timing.BATTLE_SLIDE_IN_FRAMES` (72) and `update` counts it *down* to 0 — which
is exactly why `drawBattlerPic` can multiply it straight by
`BATTLE_SLIDE_PX_PER_FRAME` and get an offset that shrinks to nothing.

`drawField` passed one into the other raw. So a **settled** battle — `introSlide`
0, which is every frame after the first 72 and every frame of a save resumed
mid-battle — asked for step 0 and got both platforms exactly where they *begin*:

| side | centre at rest | 
|---|---|
| player | 336, a 256-wide slab, so only x **208..256** on screen |
| enemy | -80, 128 wide, so **-144..-16** — entirely off the left edge |

Which is the whole of the report. The green-and-tan curve in the bottom-right
corner of the screenshot is the *left edge* of the player's platform, 272 pixels
from where it belongs, and the foe stood on nothing because its platform was off
the side of the screen. During the intro it was inverted: 36 frames remaining
asked for step 36, past the 34-step total, so the platforms sat settled while the
battlers were still travelling.

The fix is a named converter rather than an inline `total - step`, because the
frame-to-step conversion is the thing that was wrong and it should have somewhere
to be checked:

```lua
function Gen4Battle.platformSlideElapsed(battle, side)
  local total = select(side == "player" and 1 or 2,
                       Gen4Battle.platformSlideSteps())
  local frames = tonumber(battle and battle.introSlide)
  if not frames or frames <= 0 then return total end
  local all = tonumber(Timing.BATTLE_SLIDE_IN_FRAMES)
  if not all or all <= 0 then return total end
  if frames >= all then return 0 end
  return math.floor(total * (all - frames) / all + 0.5)
end
```

**No counter at all is settled, not step zero.** A headless caller, a resumed
save and every frame after the intro all arrive at that first branch, and reading
"absent" as "has not started moving" is the same bug through a different door.

The comment that had been sitting above the bug said `introSlide` *"counts UP
from 0"*. It does not, and it never did. That is the recurring fault again — a
comment that disagrees with the engine, believed instead of the code next to it.

### 2. Sinnoh had no type system at all

Scratch decodes perfectly: power 40, pp 35, accuracy 100, physical, effect 0,
typeId 0. It still did nothing recognisable, because **nothing downstream could
read its type.** Three mismatches in one chain, each invisible on its own:

* a Gen 4 **move** carried `typeId` and no `type`, and `Damage.lua` reads
  `move.type` in nine places — STAB, effectiveness, weather, held items,
  `Abilities.normalizeType`. Every Platinum move was *typeless*.
* a Gen 4 **species** carried `types = { "grass" }` in lower case, while every
  other game in this launcher is keyed `GRASS`, and `TypeChart` matches on string
  identity. Even with a chart, nothing would have matched.
* and `Gen4TypeChart.chart` returned a nested `out[attacker][defender]` map where
  `TypeChart.load` wants `matchups` as an **array** and `types` as a record per
  type. So `data.type_chart.matchups` was `nil`, and there was no
  `gen4_type_chart.lua` in the cache to load in the first place.

The result was a region where Normal hit Ghost, Water did not beat Fire and no
move ever got its own type's bonus — with no crash and no log line.

The fix is one spelling: `Gen4TypeChart.TYPES`, upper case and 0-based.
`Gen4Species.TYPES` is now `require("src.import.Gen4TypeChart").TYPES` — the same
table by *identity*, not a second list that agrees today — and `Gen4Moves.parse`
puts `type` beside `typeId`. Verified against the ROM: **110 matchups**, `NORMAL
vs GHOST = 0`, `WATER vs FIRE = 20`, `FIRE vs WATER = 5`, `GRASS vs WATER = 20`,
`ELECTRIC vs GROUND = 0`, `NORMAL vs ROCK = 5`; **471 of 471 moves typed**.

**Slot 9 is the trap.** Gen 2's unused "bird" type left a hole between `STEEL`
and `FIRE`, so every id from FIRE up is one higher than an eighteen-name list
would suggest: `FIRE` is 10 and `WATER` is **11**. I wrote `WATER` at 10 from
memory *while writing the check for this very fix*, and the check failed on my own
expectation. `SPECIAL_FROM = 10` is therefore FIRE, not WATER — it is the
pre-Gen-4 split by type, which Platinum does not use (every Gen 4 move carries
its own `class`) and which `Damage.lua` reaches only for a mod's move or a
damaged cache.

### 3. The move grid was drawn but not navigated

`BattleState:moveGridNavigate` gates the 2x2 grid arm on
`isWideBattleLayout() or gen3Layout()`. Sinnoh is neither — `gen4Layout()` is its
own predicate, because the DS screen *is* the layout and there is no narrower
cartridge shape underneath it to widen. So Gen 4 drew the four moves two to a row
and then fell through to the classic **vertical** list, where down is simply
`index + 1` — and `index + 1` from the top-left of a 2x2 is the cell to its
**right**. Left and right did nothing at all, because a vertical list has no use
for them. That is *"seems to move right when i press down"*, exactly.

One clause, no new maths: the grid this layout already draws is the grid it
should navigate.

### What the checks say

`gen4_battlescene_check.lua`: **111 → 134 checks, 0 failures.** Fifteen of the
new ones are the slide, and the first of those is the one that would have caught
the original: *a platform at rest has to be on screen.* The rest pin the
direction down, so a fix that merely clamped both ends would still fail —
including a monotone walk over all 72 frames, which catches an off-by-one in the
conversion as a step *backwards* rather than as a wrong endpoint.

**The check's own stub caught itself, twice, and both times usefully.** This tool
serves every `src.*` module it is not explicitly measuring from an `inert`
stand-in that answers every field with a function. With `src.core.Timing` inert,
`BATTLE_SLIDE_IN_FRAMES` came back as a *function*, `tonumber` made it `nil`, the
converter took its "no intro is running" branch and every platform sat settled —
so the two intro checks failed against the stand-in while the module was right. A
safe fallback is correct for play and exactly wrong for a measurement. With
`Gen4TypeChart` inert, `TYPES` was a function and indexing it *raised*, which is
the better of the two ways for a stub to be found out. Four modules are now on
the exemption list with that reasoning written beside them.

Proved to fail: passing `introSlide` in raw again, reversing the subtraction,
returning 0 instead of `total` for an absent counter, symmetrising `WATER>FIRE`,
and lower-casing one name in `TYPES`.

The rest of the sweep, unchanged: coverage 6/0, distribution world 57/0, branch
6/0, icons 9/0, party 28/0, summary 20/0, seam 162 verbs / 162 handlers, lifts
50/0, roamers 45/0; `gen4_operand_roles.py` 338 lowerings with one not
comparable; the use-before-local scanner 216 files, 0 sites, canary ok.

### These three are extractor-side and the cache is not

`Gen4TypeChart`, `Gen4Species` and `Gen4Moves` all run at **import** time. The
fixes are in the tree but the cache in `G:\Gen2Recomped` still holds the old
tables — typeless moves, lower-case species types, and no `gen4_type_chart.lua`
at all. **Platinum needs re-importing before any of the type work reaches play.**
The platform and move-grid fixes are runtime and take effect on the next launch.

### Still open

* **Move animations and FX.** Scratch shows none. Untouched by the above: the
  type chain explains why it did no damage, not why it drew nothing.
* **The backdrop decode.** Flat horizontal bands with a black stripe — the
  background stage is laying tiles out as rows of colour rather than through its
  tilemap. Evidence image sent.
* Whether the `"TURTWIG's / o!"` message is a separate fault or a symptom of the
  typeless move.
* The longer tail from `gen4_map_reach.lua`: `initturnbackcave` (20 maps, side),
  the Battle Frontier / Battle Tower save-and-link block behind one door,
  `activateregiruinsdot`, `gethour`, `messageunown`, `drawpokemonpreview`.
